irene-great-martyr.life: Irene, born Penelope in Magedon in Persia in the fourth century, was the daughter of a pagan ruler. Her tutor Apellian taught her the faith; she was baptized, took the name Irene, refused marriage and, tradition holds, led her father and many thousands to Christ. She endured repeated tortures under persecuting governors, including enclosure in heated bronze oxen, and is venerated as a Great Martyr.

theodotus-ancyra.life: Theodotus was a married innkeeper in Ancyra in Galatia during the persecution of Christians. He ransomed or secretly recovered martyrs' bodies for burial, and tradition holds that the Liturgy was celebrated in his inn after the churches were closed. After he buried seven martyred women, a fellow Christian under torture denounced him, and he was put to death. His account was written by his companion Nilus.

theodotus-ancyra-bishop.life: Theodotus lived in Ancyra in Galatia during the Diocletian persecution. He sheltered Christians, hosted their secret services, visited prisoners, paid bail, and buried martyrs' bodies, including seven women who had been drowned. Denounced to the governor, he refused to sacrifice, was tortured and beheaded. Tradition holds that a storm prevented the burning of his body, and a Christian took the relics for burial.

agabus-apostle.life: Agabus was one of the Seventy Apostles and a Christian prophet. Acts records that he foretold a great famine under Emperor Claudius and that he predicted Paul's imprisonment at Jerusalem. Tradition holds that he preached in many lands and converted pagans, and that he suffered martyrdom. He is commemorated on April 8 together with Herodion, Asyncritus, Rufus, Phlegon and Hermes.
agabus-apostle.place: Jerusalem and Antioch (per Acts); later ministry unspecified

cosmas-damian-arabia.life: Cosmas and Damian were physicians from Arabia who traveled through towns and villages preaching Christ and healing the sick without payment. In Cilicia they were arrested and brought before the governor Lysias, who had them beaten and cast into the sea. Tradition holds that an angel brought them ashore; they were then beheaded, together with Leontius, Anthimus and Eutropius, said to be their brothers.

thyrsus-leucius-philemon.life: Thyrsus, Leucius and Callinicus were martyred under Emperor Decius. Leucius rebuked the prefect Cumbricius for persecuting Christians and was tortured and executed. Thyrsus, still a catechumen, endured severe torments after refusing to sacrifice, and tradition holds that his prayers toppled a statue of Apollo. The pagan priest Callinicus, moved by what he saw, confessed Christ and was beheaded.

cornelius-centurion.life: Cornelius was a centurion at Caesarea in Palestine whose conversion is told in Acts 10: an angel directed him to summon Peter, who baptized him and his household as the first Gentile convert. Tradition holds that Peter made him a bishop and sent him to Skepsis, where his prayer toppled a temple, the local prince Demetrius and his family were baptized, and he died in old age.

synaxis-seventy-apostles.life: The Gospel of Luke records that Christ appointed seventy disciples, sent in pairs ahead of him to the towns he planned to visit. Some manuscripts give the number as seventy-two. The Church keeps this joint feast in honor of the whole company, to which tradition adds others later associated with the apostles, so those called 'of the Seventy' exceed the literal number.
synaxis-seventy-apostles.place: Judea and the wider Mediterranean world

gregory-nyssa.life: Gregory was the younger brother of Basil the Great and a Cappadocian theologian, first a teacher of rhetoric. Consecrated bishop of Nyssa about 372, he was exiled under the Arian emperor Valens, returned after 378, and took part in the Council of Constantinople in 381. His many writings earned the title 'Father of Fathers' at the Seventh Ecumenical Council. He died around 395.

veneration-chains-peter.life: This feast recalls the chains that held the Apostle Peter when Herod Agrippa imprisoned him in Jerusalem about 42, and which fell from him when an angel freed him, as told in the Acts of the Apostles. Christians kept the chains as relics. Tradition holds that they were eventually brought to Constantinople and kept in a church dedicated to Peter, where healings were reported.

apostle-timothy.life: Timothy of Lystra in Asia Minor was raised in the faith by his mother Eunice and grandmother Lois and became Paul's closest companion; two New Testament letters are addressed to him. Tradition holds that Paul made him first bishop of Ephesus and that around 97 a mob beat him to death after he opposed a pagan festival. His relics were later taken to Constantinople.

martyr-ignatius-god-bearer-translation.life: Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, was condemned under Trajan and killed by wild beasts in Rome, about 107. Christians gathered his remaining bones. The feast recalls their return to Antioch, which tradition places in 108, where his former flock received them. His letters to churches written on the journey to Rome survive; his main commemoration is December 20.

cyrus-john-unmercenaries.life: Cyrus was an Alexandrian physician who treated the sick without charge and fled to Arabia when Diocletian's persecution began, becoming a monk. John, a soldier from Edessa, left the army to join him. After they went to encourage a Christian woman, Athanasia, and her three daughters during arrest, all were seized and beheaded, about 311.

theodore-stratelates.life: Theodore was an imperial commander at Heraclea in Pontus, associated also with Euchaita, who openly confessed Christ under the emperor Licinius. Tradition holds that he smashed gold and silver idols entrusted to him and gave the metal to the poor, then survived severe tortures and crucifixion before being put to death, about 319. He is honored as a Great Martyr.

haralambos-martyr.life: Haralambos was bishop of Magnesia, in Thessaly or Asia Minor according to differing accounts, who preached openly during the persecution under Septimius Severus. Tradition holds that he endured torture despite great age, converted many, and died in 202 together with companions, including Porphyrius, Baptus and three women. He is widely venerated in Greece as a protector of health.

alexios-metropolitan-moscow.life: Alexios, born to a Moscow boyar family in the early 1300s (sources differ on the year), became a monk, then bishop of Vladimir and, about 1354, Metropolitan of Kiev and All Rus' residing in Moscow. He journeyed to the Tatar Golden Horde, where tradition holds he healed the khan's wife, founded monasteries, and died in 1378. He was glorified in 1448.

cyril-constantine-philosopher.life: Constantine, called Cyril as a monk, was born in Thessalonica and was a scholar at Constantinople. With his brother Methodius he led a mission to Moravia, translating Scripture and services into Slavonic and devising the first Slavic alphabet. He took the monastic name Cyril shortly before dying in Rome in 869. He is honored as Equal-to-the-Apostles and Teacher of the Slavs.

onesimus-apostle.life: Onesimus was a slave of Philemon of Colossae who ran away to Rome, where Paul converted him and sent him back with the letter to Philemon asking that he be received as a brother. Tradition holds that he was freed, served the Church as bishop, and was beaten to death for the faith. He is counted among the Seventy.

theodore-tyron.life: Theodore was a young Roman soldier from Pontus stationed at Amasea who, according to tradition, refused to sacrifice to the gods during the persecution about 303 and burned a pagan temple. He was tortured and burned. A later legend adds that he killed a dragon near Euchaita. He was widely venerated by the late fourth century.

leo-rome.life: Leo was Bishop of Rome from 440 to 461. His letter, the Tome, set out the doctrine of Christ's two natures against Eutyches; it was read and accepted at the Council of Chalcedon in 451. He is also remembered for persuading Attila to withdraw from Italy in 452 and for negotiating with the Vandals after Rome's sack in 455.

finding-relics-innocent-irkutsk.life: Innocent Kulchitsky, a monk of the Kiev Caves, became the first bishop of Irkutsk and worked among the Buryat and Mongol peoples of Siberia until his death in 1731. In 1764 his body was found undecayed during building work, and in 1805 the Synod ordered his relics uncovered and him numbered among the saints.

polycarp-smyrna.life: Polycarp was bishop of Smyrna and, according to Irenaeus, a disciple of the apostles. He corresponded with Ignatius of Antioch and led his church for many decades. Arrested in a persecution in his old age, probably in the mid-150s, he refused to renounce Christ, saying he had served him for eighty-six years, and was killed. An eyewitness letter from Smyrna records his martyrdom.

forty-martyrs-sebaste.life: Forty soldiers of the Roman army in Armenia refused to renounce Christ under the emperor Licinius, about 320. They were condemned to stand overnight, stripped, on a frozen lake near Sebaste. Tradition holds that one lost heart and left, and a guard who saw their endurance took his place. In the morning the martyrs died, and their remains were honorably buried.

cyril-jerusalem.life: Cyril was born in or near Jerusalem about 315, became a priest, and succeeded Maximus as bishop of Jerusalem about 350. Conflicts with Acacius of Caesarea and imperial policy led to three exiles. He is best known for his catechetical lectures, which describe how converts were instructed and baptized, and he took part in the Council of Constantinople in 381. He died in 386.

synaxis-archangel-gabriel.life: This feast, kept the day after the Annunciation, gives thanks to the Archangel Gabriel, who announced the Incarnation to the Virgin Mary. It also recalls the other appearances of Gabriel recorded in Scripture, including the visions to the prophet Daniel and the announcement to Zechariah about John the Baptist. It is held to have been added to the calendar around the ninth century.

john-climacus.life: John entered the monastery on Mount Sinai in his youth, spent years under an elder, then lived as a hermit before becoming abbot there. At the request of a neighboring abbot he wrote the Ladder of Divine Ascent, a treatise on the stages of the spiritual life which is read during Great Lent. Tradition holds he died about 649.

mary-egypt.life: Mary of Egypt, according to the life ascribed to Sophronius of Jerusalem, lived a dissolute life in Alexandria before being turned to repentance at Jerusalem. She withdrew to the desert beyond the Jordan for decades. The monk Zosimas met her there, heard her story, and gave her communion; she died soon after. Dates of her death are uncertain.

martin-pope-rome.life: Martin was elected Bishop of Rome in 649 and held a council at the Lateran that condemned Monothelitism and the emperor Constans II's decree, the Typos. Constans had him arrested and taken to Constantinople, tried, and exiled to Cherson in the Crimea, where he died in 655 after suffering hardship. Both East and West honor him as a martyr and confessor.

theodore-sykeote.life: Theodore was born at Sykeon in Galatia in the mid-sixth century and lived as an ascetic from boyhood, visiting the Holy Land and becoming a monk. Around 590 he was made bishop of Anastasiopolis, and some years later he returned to the monastic life. He was known for healing and exorcism. He died in 613. A biography by his disciple Eleusios survives.

james-zebedee.life: James, son of Zebedee and brother of John, was a fisherman called by Jesus to be one of the Twelve and was among the three disciples present at the Transfiguration. The Acts of the Apostles records that Herod Agrippa had him killed by the sword, about 44, making him the first apostle martyred. Later tradition links him to preaching in Spain.

athanasius-alexandria.life: Athanasius was born about 297 in Alexandria, attended the Council of Nicaea as a deacon, and became bishop of Alexandria in 328. He was a leading defender of the Nicene teaching on Christ's divinity against the Arians and was exiled five times for it. His writings include On the Incarnation. He died in 373. His principal feast is January 18.

simon-zealot-apostle.life: Simon the Zealot was one of the Twelve Apostles, named in the Gospel lists with the epithet 'Zealot'. Tradition holds that he came from Cana of Galilee and, after Pentecost, preached in Africa or elsewhere and died by crucifixion. Sources vary on where he preached and how he died, and identification with the bridegroom at Cana is a later tradition.

nina-georgia.life: Nina, called Nino in Georgian tradition, was a Cappadocian Christian who came as a captive to the kingdom of Iberia, in present-day Georgia. Tradition holds that her prayers healed the queen and, after a hunting mishap, led King Mirian to seek baptism for himself and his people. She is honored as Equal-to-the-Apostles and Enlightener of Georgia, and died around 335.

agape-irene-chionia.life: Agape, Irene and Chionia were three Christian sisters who, tradition holds, lived near Aquileia and were brought before the emperor Diocletian about the turn of the fourth century. They would not deny Christ and were imprisoned and tortured. Agape and Chionia were burned, and Irene was killed by an arrow. Accounts differ on the details of their sufferings.

cyril-methodius-slavs.life: Brothers from Thessalonica, Cyril and Methodius were sent as missionaries to the Slavic peoples of Moravia in the ninth century. They devised a Slavic alphabet, translated Scripture and liturgical texts into the Slavonic tongue, and defended this work before Rome. Cyril died in Rome in 869, and Methodius, later an archbishop, died in 885. Slavic Churches honor them as teachers of their peoples.

pachomius-great.life: Pachomius was born in Upper Egypt around 292 and came to the faith after serving in the Roman army. Withdrawing to the desert, he gathered disciples at Tabennisi and gave them a common rule of life, work and prayer, which established communal monasticism. His communities spread across the Thebaid. He died in 348, and later monastic movements drew on his example.

cyril-alexandria-bishop.life: Cyril served as Patriarch of Alexandria from 412 until his death in 444. He was the chief opponent of Nestorius, who resisted calling Mary the Theotokos, and he led the argument at the Third Ecumenical Council of Ephesus in 431, which affirmed that title. His many letters, commentaries and theological treatises shaped later teaching on the person of Christ.

bartholomew-barnabas-apostles.life: Bartholomew was one of the Twelve; tradition holds that he preached in the East, including Armenia, and was martyred there. Barnabas, a Levite from Cyprus, accompanied Paul on his first missionary journey and spoke for him before the Church at Jerusalem, as Acts relates. Tradition says he was killed at Salamis on Cyprus. The Church keeps their memory together on this day.

onuphrius-great.life: Onuphrius was a hermit of the Egyptian desert, living in the fourth or fifth century. According to the account of the monk Paphnutius, who found him, he had lived alone for about sixty years, clothed only by his own hair, sustained by a date palm and a spring, and receiving communion in solitude. Paphnutius buried him after his death.

jude-apostle-brother-lord.life: Jude, called a brother of the Lord, is honored as author of the Epistle of Jude and as an apostle who preached in Judea, Syria and Mesopotamia. Tradition holds that he was martyred in Armenia. Note that the calendar distinguishes him from Thaddaeus of the Twelve, who is kept on June 21.

eusebius-samosata.life: Eusebius was Bishop of Samosata in Syria and a firm supporter of the Nicene faith against the Arians. He worked closely with Meletius of Antioch, was exiled by the Arian emperor Valens, and after Valens died traveled to appoint Orthodox bishops. Around 380, as he entered a town for this purpose, an Arian woman hit him with a roof tile, and he died of the wound.

synaxis-twelve-apostles.life: The Church gathers on this day, following the feast of Peter and Paul, to honor all twelve apostles whom Christ chose and sent out to preach the Gospel. Matthias was added to their number after the loss of Judas Iscariot, as Acts records. The commemoration recalls their shared witness and the spread of the Church through their labors.

deposition-robe-theotokos.life: This feast recalls the placing of the Virgin Mary's robe in a church at Blachernae, near Constantinople. According to the tradition, two patricians brought it from Palestine during the reign of Leo I (457-474) and housed it in a shrine there. The robe was long kept at Blachernae and was venerated as a protection for the city.

prokopios-caesarea-martyr.life: Prokopios, a Christian official of Palestinian Caesarea, was arrested in the persecution under Diocletian and refused to offer sacrifice. He was beheaded around 303. Tradition holds that he was born in Jerusalem and was converted on a journey to Syria. He became one of the best-known military and great martyrs of the Eastern Church.

euphemia-great-martyr.life: Euphemia, a young Christian of Chalcedon who was martyred around 303, was honored by a church there that held her relics. This July feast recalls the Council of Chalcedon in 451: tradition holds that the competing confessions of faith were placed in her tomb, and that the Orthodox text was found in her hand. Her martyrdom is kept on September 16.

vladimir-equal-apostles.life: Vladimir, Prince of Novgorod and then Grand Prince of Kiev, ruled from 978 until his death in 1015. Around 988 he accepted baptism from Constantinople and led the people of Kievan Rus to the Christian faith. He worked to build churches and to care for the poor. The Church honors him as Equal-to-the-Apostles for bringing Christianity to the Russian lands.

royal-martyrs-russia.life: Nicholas II, the last Russian emperor, his wife Alexandra, and their five children Olga, Tatiana, Maria, Anastasia and Alexei were shot by Bolshevik guards at Ekaterinburg on the night of 16-17 July 1918, after the family had been imprisoned. The Russian Church Abroad glorified them in 1981, and the Moscow Patriarchate in 2000, as passion-bearers who met their ordeal with humility.

mary-magdalene-equal-apostles.life: Mary Magdalene was a woman of Magdala who followed Jesus, stood near the Cross, and went to the tomb with the myrrh-bearing women. The Gospels name her the first witness to the empty tomb and the risen Christ. The Church calls her Equal-to-the-Apostles. Tradition holds that she later preached and died at Ephesus.

dormition-anna-mother-theotokos.life: Anna is remembered as the wife of Joachim and mother of the Virgin Mary. Her name comes not from the canonical Gospels but from early tradition, notably the Protoevangelium of James. This feast marks her repose. Church tradition holds that she and Joachim died while Mary was still young, and Anna is invoked by couples hoping for children.

panteleimon-great-martyr.life: Panteleimon was a physician of Nicomedia, born of a pagan father and a Christian mother. Tradition holds that he became a Christian and healed the sick without payment, which led to his denunciation. He was martyred under Diocletian or Maximian around 305. The Church honors him as a Great Martyr and as a Holy Unmercenary healer.

procession-cross-maccabees.life: On August 1 the Byzantine Church marked the carrying of the Cross relic from the imperial treasury through the streets of Constantinople, a custom that began a fortnight of veneration before the Dormition. The day also commemorates the seven Maccabee brothers, their mother Solomonia and their teacher Eleazar, who were martyred in 168 BC under Antiochus Epiphanes rather than eat forbidden food.

matthias-apostle-august.life: Matthias was a disciple who had accompanied Jesus from his baptism through the Resurrection. After Judas Iscariot's fall, the apostles cast lots between two candidates, and Matthias was numbered among the Twelve, as Acts 1 describes. Traditions about his later mission and death differ; some place his preaching in Judea and in regions near the Black Sea.

icon-not-made-by-hands.life: According to tradition, Jesus pressed a cloth to his face and sent the resulting image to King Abgar of Edessa, who was healed. The cloth, known as the Mandylion, was kept at Edessa for centuries. In 944 it was taken to Constantinople, and this feast commemorates its arrival there. The image is regarded as the first icon of Christ.

bartholomew-titus-apostles.life: Bartholomew, one of the Twelve, is remembered in tradition as a missionary who preached in the East and died a martyr in Armenia. Titus was a Gentile convert and co-worker of Paul, to whom Paul addressed an epistle, and is traditionally counted among the Seventy and as first bishop of Crete. This day honors both apostles.

tikhon-zadonsk.life: Tikhon was born Timothy Sokolov in 1724, near Novgorod, and became Bishop of Voronezh in 1763. After a few years he retired to the monastery at Zadonsk because of ill health. There he wrote spiritual works and helped the poor until his death in 1783. The Russian Church glorified him in 1861.

deposition-belt-theotokos.life: The Church recalls the placing of the Virgin Mary's belt in a shrine at Blachernae, Constantinople. Tradition holds that the belt passed to Thomas at the Dormition and was brought from Cappadocia to Constantinople, where it was kept in a sealed chest. Accounts differ on whether the feast marks its arrival under Arcadius or the later healing of Empress Zoe.

archangel-michael-miracle-chonae.life: At Colossae in Phrygia stood a church of the Archangel Michael beside a spring with healing waters. According to tradition, pagan opponents diverted two rivers to flood it, but Michael appeared and opened a chasm in the earth that swallowed the water. The place was afterwards called Chonae, meaning funnels, and the church was spared.

euphemia-all-praised-september.life: Euphemia of Chalcedon, daughter of a senator, was arrested during the persecution of Diocletian for refusing to sacrifice to Ares. She was tortured and died in the arena around 303. Her tomb became a pilgrimage site, and at the Council of Chalcedon in 451 the bishops met in her church. Her feast on September 16 marks her martyrdom.

eustathios-thespesia-companions.life: Eustathios, born Placidas, was a Roman general who, according to tradition, converted after seeing a cross between the antlers of a stag. He, his wife Theopiste and their sons were baptized and later endured long separations and trials before being reunited. Under Emperor Hadrian they refused to sacrifice to idols and were martyred together.

thekla-equal-apostles.life: Thekla of Iconium is known chiefly from the second-century Acts of Paul and Thecla. According to that account, she heard Paul preach, refused marriage and was condemned, yet survived trials by fire and beasts. The Church honors her as first woman martyr and Equal-to-the-Apostles. Tradition holds that she later taught and lived near Seleucia.

thomas-maleon.life: Thomas, a successful military commander, left the world to become a monk and, with his elders' blessing, lived as a hermit on Mount Maleon in Lakonia in the Peloponnese. Tradition holds that the prophet Elijah led him there; people sought his counsel and the sick were healed. He reposed in the tenth century, and part of his relics rest at Monemvasia and Sparta. He is commemorated with Acacius, a sixth-century Sinai monk of the Ladder, known for his obedience to a harsh elder.

gregory-illuminator-armenia.life: Born of Parthian stock and raised as a Christian in Cappadocia, Gregory returned to Armenia and was imprisoned by King Tiridates III for his faith. Tradition holds that the king, later healed and converted, was baptized by him around 301, making Armenia the first Christian kingdom. Gregory became its first catholicos and organized the church there, and is venerated as its enlightener.

thomas-apostle-october.life: One of the Twelve, Thomas is remembered in John's Gospel for doubting the report of the Resurrection until he saw and touched the risen Christ, then confessing him as Lord and God. Tradition holds that he preached in the East, reaching Parthia and India, and was killed near Mylapore. His principal commemoration is July 7; October 6 is a further commemoration.

james-alphaeus-apostle.life: James son of Alphaeus is named among the Twelve in the lists of the Gospels and Acts, and little else is recorded of him in Scripture. Tradition holds that he preached in Judea and then in other lands, and was put to death for the faith. Sources differ on whether he is the same as James the Less.

paraskeva-serbia.life: Paraskeva was born at Epivates in Thrace, near the Sea of Marmara, and left home to live as a hermit, spending years in the Jordan desert. She returned to her homeland and died there in prayer. Her relics were moved several times, resting in Bulgaria, Serbia and Constantinople, and since 1641 in Iași, Romania. She is venerated across the Balkans.

john-kronstadt.life: Born in a village near Arkhangelsk, John served as a priest at St. Andrew's Cathedral in Kronstadt from 1855. He was known for caring for the poor, founding a house of industry, and urging frequent communion. Many sought his prayers for healing, and his diary My Life in Christ was widely read. The Russian Orthodox Church canonized him in 1990.

james-brother-lord.life: Called the Just, James was the first bishop of Jerusalem and is identified in the New Testament as the Lord's brother; Orthodox tradition understands him as a son of Joseph by an earlier marriage. He presided over the apostolic council described in Acts 15 and wrote the Epistle of James. Josephus and early Christian writers report that he was killed in Jerusalem around 62.

cosmas-damian-asia.life: Cosmas and Damian were brothers from Asia Minor, sons of Theodota, who practiced medicine and refused payment for healing the sick, which is why they are called unmercenaries. Tradition holds they led a quiet life of service and died peacefully, unlike the better-known Roman pair. This commemoration is the one kept on November 1.

joannicius-great.life: Born in Bithynia, Joannicius was first a swineherd and then a soldier before entering the monastic life as a young man. He lived for decades as a hermit on Mount Olympus, was known for supporting the veneration of icons during the iconoclast period, and counseled many visitors, among them patriarchs. He died at about ninety-two.

paul-patriarch-cp.life: Paul became Patriarch of Constantinople in the 330s and defended the Nicene faith against the Arians. Supported by the western emperor but opposed by Constantius II and his rivals, he was deposed and exiled more than once. Tradition holds he was killed in exile at Cucusus in Armenia around 350. His relics were later brought back to Constantinople.

john-the-merciful.life: Born in Cyprus, John served as Patriarch of Alexandria in the early seventh century and became known for his generosity to the poor, founding hospices and distributing the church's wealth. When Persian forces approached Alexandria in 614 he left for Cyprus, where he died, perhaps in 616 or 619. He is called 'the Almsgiver' or 'the Merciful'.

gregory-wonderworker.life: Gregory was a native of Neocaesarea in Pontus who studied in Caesarea under Origen, then returned home and became its first bishop. Tradition says almost no Christians were in the city when he arrived and few pagans remained at his death. He is credited with many miracles, which gave him his epithet, and a doctrinal creed attributed to him.

amphilochius-iconium.life: A cousin of Gregory the Theologian, Amphilochius first worked as a lawyer, then became an ascetic and was made Bishop of Iconium around 373. He was a friend of Basil the Great, who wrote On the Holy Spirit at his request. He took part in the Council of Constantinople in 381 and opposed those who denied the divinity of the Spirit.

great-martyr-catherine.life: According to tradition, Catherine was a highly educated young woman of Alexandria who confessed Christ and defeated pagan philosophers in debate, then suffered martyrdom under a pagan emperor, probably in the early fourth century. Her written Life dates from later centuries and early evidence is thin, but her veneration is ancient and widespread, and she is honored as a patroness of learning.

clement-rome.life: Clement became bishop of Rome in the late first century and is traditionally listed as a successor of Peter. He is credited with the First Epistle to the Corinthians, which urged the Corinthian church to restore order. Tradition holds that he was banished to the Crimea under Trajan and died there as a martyr, around the year 100.

leavetaking-entrance-theotokos.life: The Leavetaking is the final day of the Entrance of the Theotokos, which is celebrated on November 21. The feast recalls the tradition, found in the Protoevangelium of James, that Joachim and Anna brought the child Mary at the age of three to the Temple in Jerusalem, where she was dedicated to God and raised.

james-the-persian.life: James was a Christian soldier in the Persian court of Yazdegerd I who, tradition says, renounced the faith to keep his rank. Rebuked by his mother and wife, he repented. Under Bahram V he was tortured and cut into pieces joint by joint, hence the name Intercisus, and he died in 421 praying. He is honored as a great martyr.

barbara-great-martyr.life: Tradition holds that Barbara, the daughter of a wealthy pagan named Dioscorus, was confined in a tower, secretly became a Christian, and was baptized. When she would not renounce her faith, she was tortured and then beheaded, reportedly by her own father. Accounts place her at Heliopolis or Nicomedia, around 290 to 306; the details are legendary and sources differ.

john-damascene.life: Born in Damascus to a Christian family that served the Muslim caliphs, John left public office to become a monk at Mar Saba near Jerusalem. He wrote in defense of holy icons against the iconoclasts and composed a major theological summary, the Fount of Knowledge. He also wrote canons and other church hymns. He died around 749.

ambrose-milan.life: Ambrose was governor of northern Italy when, in 374, the people of Milan chose him as bishop while he was still unbaptized. He defended the Nicene faith against Arianism, preached widely, and wrote hymns and theological works. He helped bring Augustine to baptism in 387. December 7 marks his consecration; he died in 397.

conception-theotokos-anna.life: This feast commemorates the conception of the Virgin Mary by Anna and Joachim. According to the Protoevangelium of James, the couple had long been childless and received the promise of a child. The Church celebrates the event on December 9, nine months before the Nativity of the Theotokos on September 8.

daniel-stylite.life: Born in Mesopotamia, Daniel became a monk young and visited Symeon the Stylite. He later settled near Constantinople, where he lived for thirty-three years on a pillar, praying in all weather. Emperors, including Leo I, and many ordinary people sought his counsel. He died at the age of about eighty-four.

prophet-daniel-three-youths.life: Daniel was a Jewish captive taken to Babylon in the sixth century BC who served at the royal court and interpreted dreams and visions. His companions Ananias, Azarias and Misael refused to worship the king's golden image and were cast into a fiery furnace but were preserved. Daniel was himself delivered from a den of lions. Their story is told in the Book of Daniel.

ignatius-god-bearer.life: Ignatius was bishop of Antioch in Syria, said to have been a disciple of the apostle John. Condemned during the reign of Trajan, he was taken under guard to Rome, writing letters to several churches on the way that urge unity under the bishop. He was martyred in Rome, killed by wild beasts, around 107.

great-martyr-anastasia.life: Born in Rome, Anastasia was a Christian woman who, tradition says, secretly visited and aided Christians imprisoned under Diocletian. After her husband's death she gave her wealth to the suffering. She was arrested and put to death around 304. She is called the Deliverer from Potions for her help to the afflicted.

twenty-thousand-martyrs-nicomedia.life: During the persecution under Diocletian and Maximian, a large group of Christians gathered in a church at Nicomedia on the day of the Nativity. Tradition says the emperor had the building surrounded and set on fire after they refused to sacrifice to idols, and about twenty thousand perished. The year is given as 302 or 303, and the figure is traditional.

holy-innocents.life: The Gospel of Matthew reports that Herod the Great, hearing of a newborn king, ordered the killing of the male children of Bethlehem and its surrounding area. Joseph took the child Jesus to Egypt to escape. Orthodox tradition honors these children as martyrs and numbers them at fourteen thousand, though the Gospel gives no figure.

prophet-malachi.life: Malachi was the last of the Old Testament prophets, active about four centuries before Christ, after the Jews returned from the Babylonian captivity. His name means "angel" or "messenger", and his book closes the Old Testament canon. In it he rebukes the people and foretells the coming of Christ, of His Forerunner, and of the Last Judgment.

gordius-caesarea.life: Gordius, born into a Christian family at Caesarea in Cappadocia, served as a centurion. When persecution came in the early fourth century he withdrew to the desert to prepare for confessing Christ. He then presented himself at a pagan festival in Caesarea, declared himself a Christian before the governor, endured torture, and was beheaded.

forefeast-theophany.life: The Forefeast of Theophany, on the eve of the feast, is kept with strict fasting, the Royal Hours, and thirteen readings at Vespers. The day also remembers Bishop Theopemptus of Nicomedia and Theonas, who suffered there in 303 under Diocletian. Theopemptus survived a furnace, starvation and poison; Theonas, converted by this, was buried alive, and Theopemptus was beheaded.

george-chozebite.life: George was born on Cyprus toward the end of the sixth century and travelled to Palestine to venerate the holy places. He entered the monastery of Chozeba, between the Jordan and Jerusalem, and later became its abbot. He set the monks an example in fasting and vigil, and he died in peace.

domnica-constantinople.life: Domnica lived in Constantinople in the time of Emperor Theodosius the Great and Patriarch Nectarius, and entered a women's monastery there. Her strict asceticism was accompanied by healings and prophecy, and her example drew many in the capital toward concern for the soul. She died in old age as a virgin, around 474.

martyr-polyeuctus.life: Polyeuctus was a Roman soldier at Melitene in Armenia and a friend of the Christian Nearchus. After a vision of Christ clothing him in a radiant garment, he tore up the imperial edict demanding sacrifice and smashed idols carried in a procession. He was beheaded, the first martyr of Melitene, and a church there was later built in his honor.

tatiana-rome.life: Tatiana, daughter of a Roman consul, became a deaconess in Rome and served the sick and the poor. Arrested as a Christian in the reign of Alexander Severus, she was taken to a temple of Apollo, where tradition holds that the idol fell at her prayer. She endured many tortures and was beheaded, together with her father.

leavetaking-theophany.life: The Leavetaking on January 14 closes the festal period of Theophany, the Baptism of Christ. The feast's service is repeated, with several festal elements omitted: the entrance, festal readings, litya, blessing of loaves, and at Matins the polyeleos and festal Gospel. At the Liturgy the festal antiphons are not sung, and the day's own Epistle and Gospel are read.

paul-theban-john-huts.life: Paul of Thebes, born in Egypt about 227, fled into the desert during the Decian persecution and lived in a cave for decades; he is honored as the first hermit. Anthony the Great, guided by revelation, visited him and buried him after his death in 341. John Calabytes, born to a wealthy family in Constantinople, became a monk, then lived unrecognized in a hut at his parents' gate until his death.

macarius-egypt.life: Macarius was born in Egypt in the early fourth century and, widowed young, took up the ascetic life under an elder in the desert. He became a disciple of Anthony the Great, was ordained priest at forty, and led the monks of Skete. Falsely accused of fathering a child, he bore the slander humbly and withdrew. He is counted among the greatest Desert Fathers.

maximus-confessor.life: Maximus, born about 580, served as chief secretary to Emperor Heraclius before becoming a monk at Chrysopolis, where he was later abbot. He opposed Monothelitism in preaching and writing and took part in the Lateran Council of 649. Arrested under Constans II, he had his tongue and right hand cut off, and was exiled, dying in 662.

clement-ancyra-agathangelus.life: Clement, born at Ancyra in Galatia, became bishop there while still young. Under Diocletian he was arrested and tortured repeatedly over many years, yet drew many to the faith. His disciple Agathangelus joined him and was beheaded. Clement was beheaded on January 23 with the deacons Christopher and Chariton as he stood at the altar in a cave church.

xenia-rome.life: Xenia, baptized Eusebia, was the daughter of a Roman senator who fled an arranged marriage with two servants. She settled at Milassa in Caria, where she built a church of Saint Stephen and founded a women's monastery, and was made a deaconess. She aided the poor and the grieving and died about 450; tradition holds that a luminous cross appeared over her funeral.

xenophon-family.life: Xenophon and his wife Mary were wealthy, devout citizens of Constantinople. When their sons Arcadius and John were shipwrecked on the way to study at Beirut, the brothers were cast ashore separately and each became a monk. Their parents, believing them dead, went on pilgrimage and found them at Jerusalem. The family then lived as monastics, and all four are remembered as wonderworkers.

tryphon-martyr.life: Tryphon was born in Lampsacus in Phrygia and was granted gifts of healing and exorcism, including the healing of the daughter of Emperor Gordian. In the persecution of Decius he was arrested, tortured, and beheaded at Nicaea about 250. His relics were taken to his native village and later to Constantinople and Rome.

simeon-god-receiver-anna.life: Simeon was the righteous elder who, according to Luke's Gospel, took the infant Christ in his arms in the Temple on the fortieth day after the Nativity and blessed Him. Tradition holds that he was among the Septuagint translators and had been promised he would not die before seeing the Messiah. Anna, a prophetess and widow of great age, served in the Temple and spoke of the Child to all awaiting redemption.

isidore-pelusiot.life: Isidore was born at Alexandria to a noble family, a relative of Archbishop Theophilus and of Saint Cyril. He withdrew to the mountain near Pelusium in Egypt, was ordained a priest, and became known for wisdom, asceticism and preaching. Over two thousand of his letters survive. He supported John Chrysostom and urged Cyril to restore his name to the church diptychs. He died around 436.

agatha-catania.life: Agatha was a Christian girl of about fifteen from Sicily. During the persecution of Decius she was brought to trial at Catania before the prefect Quintianus, who coveted her wealth and beauty. She refused to sacrifice, endured cruel tortures, and tradition holds that the Apostle Peter healed her in prison. After an earthquake the people demanded an end to her torments, and she died in prison about 251.

bucolus-smyrna.life: Bucolus was a disciple of the Apostle John the Theologian and became the first bishop of Smyrna in Asia Minor. He converted and baptized many pagans and guarded his flock against heresy. He died in peace between 100 and 105, entrusting the church to Saint Polycarp. A myrtle tree is said to have grown at his grave and healed the sick.

parthenius-lampsacus.life: Parthenius, son of a deacon of Melitopolis in Asia Minor, was unlettered but learned Scripture by attending services, and gave his fishing earnings to the poor. Ordained a presbyter, he was made Bishop of Lampsacus in 325 under Constantine the Great, and obtained the emperor's leave to tear down pagan temples and build a church. He was renowned for healings and exorcisms.

leavetaking-presentation.life: The Leavetaking of the Meeting of the Lord concludes the festal period of the Presentation of Christ in the Temple. It usually falls on February 9 but may be moved if the feast occurs during the Triodion, in which case the Typikon is consulted. Normally the feast's service is repeated, without the entrance, festal readings, litya at Vespers, or polyeleos and festal Gospel at Matins.

blase-sebaste.life: Blaise was bishop of Sebaste under Diocletian and Licinius. He encouraged and visited imprisoned Christians, then hid in a cave on Mount Argeos, where wild animals are said to have gathered to be blessed and healed. Captured by the governor Agrilaus, he was tortured, refused to renounce Christ, and was beheaded about 316. His relics were later carried to the West.

martinian-caesarea.life: Martinian withdrew at eighteen to the wilderness near Caesarea in Palestine and lived there in ascetic silence for twenty-five years. Tempted by a woman, he stood in a fire to master the temptation; the woman, Zoe, repented and became a nun. He later lived on a rocky island, left it when another woman was shipwrecked there, and wandered until he died at Athens about 422.

pamphilius-caesarea.life: Pamphilius, a native of Beirut educated at Alexandria, was a priest at Caesarea in Palestine who corrected and copied New Testament manuscripts and gave them away. In the Diocletian persecution he was arrested with the deacon Valens, Paul, and five Egyptian youths, and all were beheaded. Four others, Porphyrius, Seleucus, Theodulus and Julian, suffered at the same time, making twelve martyrs.

archippus-apostle.life: Archippus, counted among the Seventy Apostles, was a companion of Paul, who names him in the Epistle to Philemon and in Colossians. He is linked with the church at Colossae in Phrygia and is commemorated with Philemon and Apphia. According to tradition he was put to death for the faith under Nero, though sources differ on the manner of his death and on his relation to Philemon.

leo-catania.life: Leo was born in Ravenna to a noble family and became Bishop of Catania in Sicily, known for charity to the poor, orphans and widows, and for opposing heresy. He is remembered for confronting the sorcerer Heliodorus, whom tradition says he led into a fire that consumed the sorcerer but left the bishop unharmed. Invited to Constantinople by the emperors, he died in peace in 785.

timothy-symbola.life: Timothy, of Italian descent, became a monk at the Symbola monastery in Bithynia, near Mount Olympus, and was a disciple of Theoctistus and of Saint Platon of Studion. He was granted gifts of healing the sick and casting out unclean spirits, and spent many years as a hermit praying in the wilderness. He died at a great age in 795.

tarasius-patriarch-constantinople.life: Tarasius, born in Constantinople of a distinguished family, rose to be senator and imperial secretary under Constantine VI and Empress Irene. Though still a layman, he was chosen patriarch in 784 on condition that a council address iconoclasm, and he presided at the Seventh Ecumenical Council at Nicaea in 787, which confirmed the veneration of icons. He governed the Church twenty-two years, aided the poor, and died in 806.

porphyry-gaza.life: Porphyrius, born at Thessalonica around 346, lived as a monk in the Egyptian desert and the Jordan wilderness before being ordained in Jerusalem and made keeper of the Holy Cross. In 395 he became Bishop of Gaza, a largely pagan city, where he led many to baptism and, through an imperial edict of 401, obtained the destruction of pagan temples and a new church. He died in 420.

procopius-decapolites.life: Procopius lived in the Decapolis region east of the Sea of Galilee in the eighth century and became a monk. When Emperor Leo the Isaurian began persecuting the veneration of icons, he defended it, explaining that icons are venerated, not worshipped. He was tortured and imprisoned with Saint Basil until Leo's death, then lived peacefully, dying in old age around 750.

basil-confessor.life: Basil was a monk who suffered under the iconoclast emperor Leo the Isaurian (717-741). With his companion Procopius of Decapolis he was tortured and imprisoned for venerating icons, and both were freed after the emperor's death. They then resumed their monastic labors, instructing many in the faith. Basil died peacefully in 750.

martyr-eudokia.life: Eudokia was a wealthy, immoral pagan of Heliopolis in Phoenicia who was moved to repentance after overhearing a monk read about the Last Judgment. She was baptized, gave away her wealth, entered a monastery and later led it. Accounts say she was beheaded for her faith by the governor, and she is remembered both as a penitent and as a martyr.

eutropius-cleonicus-basiliscus.life: These three companions of Saint Theodore the Recruit suffered at Amasea in Pontus around 308. Basiliscus was Theodore's nephew. After Theodore's death they were imprisoned, where they preached to fellow prisoners, and were later tortured by the governor Asclepiodotus. Eutropius and Cleonicus were crucified on March 3. Basiliscus was executed later, at Komana, and is also remembered on May 22.

gerasimus-jordan.life: Gerasimus was born in Lycia, became a monk, and went to the Thebaid before settling by the Jordan in Palestine around 450, where he founded a monastery with a strict rule of solitude on weekdays and common worship on weekends. Early in life he inclined to the Monophysite error but returned to the faith with the help of Euthymius the Great. Tradition holds that a lion served him and died at his grave.

mark-the-ascetic.life: Mark the Ascetic was a monk of the Nitrian desert in Egypt in the fifth century, remembered for his abstinence and his knowledge of Scripture. Nine of his thirty discourses survive, three of them in the English Philokalia. Byzantine readers valued his writings so highly that a saying urged people to sell everything and buy Mark. He was noted for gentleness and purity of soul.

forty-two-martyrs-ammoria.life: When the Byzantine city of Amorion fell to Arab forces in 838, forty-two of its officers were taken captive to Syria. During some seven years of imprisonment, they refused offers and threats aimed at making them renounce Christ and accept Islam. They were finally beheaded one by one, according to OCA about 845, and their bodies were thrown into the Euphrates. Among them are named Theodore, Callistus, Constantine, Theophilus and Basoes.

hieromartyrs-cherson.life: Seven bishops carried the Gospel to Cherson in the Crimea and the Black Sea region in the fourth century. Ephraim and Basil came from Jerusalem under Diocletian, and both were killed. Eugene, Elpidius and Agathodorus arrived later and were stoned. Aetherius governed the church in peace under Constantine, and Capiton, according to tradition, walked unharmed in a furnace. Capiton was later drowned. All are commemorated together.

theophylact-nicomedia.life: Theophylactus was a disciple of Patriarch Tarasius and was made Bishop of Nicomedia, where he built churches and hospices, gave alms and cared for lepers. Under the Iconoclast emperor Leo the Armenian he denounced the heresy and foretold the emperor's swift death. For this he was exiled to the fortress of Strobilus, where he lived about thirty years and died around 845. His relics were later returned to Nicomedia.

martyr-codratus-corinth.life: Codratus (spelled Quadratus by OCA) is said to have been born in the wilderness near Corinth, to have studied medicine, and to have healed the sick. Under Decius, about 250, he and companions including Cyprian, Dionysius, Anectus, Paul and Crescens were tortured and beheaded. Other disciples named in the account, such as Claudius and Diodorus, also suffered at Corinth.

sophronius-jerusalem.life: Sophronius was born in Damascus, studied philosophy, and became a monk at the monastery of Saint Theodosius near Jerusalem, where he was the spiritual child of John Moschus; together they compiled the Spiritual Meadow. He served as Patriarch of Jerusalem from 634 and opposed the Monothelite teaching. He died around 638 as Muslim forces took Jerusalem. He also wrote the Life of Mary of Egypt and hymns.

theophanes-confessor.life: Theophanes was born at Constantinople around 759 into a noble family, entered monastic life with his wife's consent, and became abbot of a monastery at Sigriane. He took part in the Seventh Ecumenical Council in 787 and wrote a Chronographia covering the years 285-813. When Leo the Armenian revived Iconoclasm he refused to yield, was imprisoned, and died around 818 as a confessor.

nikephoros-patriarch-constantinople.life: This commemoration marks the return of the relics of Patriarch Nikephoros to Constantinople in 846. He became patriarch in 806, defended the icons, and was exiled by Leo the Armenian in 815 to Prokonnis, where he died in 828. His relics were found incorrupt, placed briefly in Hagia Sophia, then in the Church of the Holy Apostles. His main feast is June 2.

benedict-nursia.life: Benedict was born in Nursia in Italy around 480, studied briefly in Rome, and withdrew to a cave at Subiaco, where disciples gathered around him. He founded monasteries, most famously Monte Cassino, and wrote a Rule drawing on Eastern monastic experience and John Cassian. His Rule long shaped Western monasticism. He died in 547, having foretold his death. The Orthodox Church commemorates him today.
benedict-nursia.place: Nursia, Subiaco and Monte Cassino, Italy

sabin-egypt.life: Sabinus was the administrator of Hermopolis in Egypt. During Diocletian's persecution he hid in a remote place, praying and fasting, until a beggar whom he had helped betrayed him for two gold pieces. He and six other Christians were arrested, tortured, and drowned in the Nile around 287.

alexios-man-of-god.life: According to tradition, Alexios was born to a pious Roman family, left his bride on his wedding night and lived as a beggar at Edessa for about seventeen years. He later returned to Rome and lived unrecognized in his father's house for another seventeen years. His identity was revealed only at his death, said to be in 411. He is venerated as the Man of God.

chrysanthos-daria.life: Chrysanthus, from a pagan Roman family, came to Christ by reading the Gospels and was baptized by the presbyter Carpophorus. He persuaded his wife Daria, a priestess of Minerva, to the faith and they lived in celibacy. Arrested under Emperor Numerian, they were tortured, and were then buried alive. The tribune Claudius and his household, converted by their witness, were also executed.

james-confessor.life: James was drawn to asceticism from youth, entered the Studite monastery in Constantinople, and was later raised to the see of Catania in Sicily. In the reign of the Iconoclast emperor Constantine V Copronymus he was pressed to abandon the veneration of icons, and was starved, beaten and imprisoned for refusing. He died in exile and is honored as a confessor.

basil-ancyra-presbyter.life: Basil was a presbyter of Ancyra in Galatia who preached against the Arians, was deposed by a local Arian council, and was reinstated by a council of 230 bishops. Under Julian the Apostate he confessed Christ before the emperor and was tortured. He died of his wounds, according to OCA on June 29, 362; his commemoration was moved to March 22. He is distinct from Basil of Ancyra, a layman, on January 1.

nikon-and-companions.life: Nikon was born in Naples to a pagan father and Christian mother, served as a soldier, and was baptized after calling on Christ in battle. He became a monk and then a bishop, and moved with many monks to Sicily. During the persecution of Decius, the governor Quintilian had his companions beheaded, and Nikon was tortured and then killed, according to the account. The number of companions is given as 199 or 190.

forefeast-annunciation.life: The Forefeast, or Prefeast, of the Annunciation is a single day of preparation on March 24 before the feast of the Annunciation to the Theotokos on March 25, nine months before the Nativity of Christ. Because the feast falls in Great Lent, it has no afterfeast. The Synaxis of the Archangel Gabriel follows on March 26.

matrona-thessalonica.life: Matrona was a slave in Thessalonica to Pautila, the Jewish wife of a military commander. Because Matrona kept attending the Christian church, her mistress beat her, bound her and shut her in a closet; tradition says she was repeatedly found free. She died from the beatings, her body was thrown from the roof, and Christians buried her. Bishop Alexander later built a church over her relics.

hilarion-new-pelekete.life: Hilarion was a hermit for many years, then priest and abbot of the Pelekete monastery near the Dardanelles, known for healing and clairvoyance. During the persecution of icon veneration he and his monks were attacked; OCA dates this to Holy Thursday 754. He died for the veneration of icons and also left spiritual writings.

mark-bishop-arethusa.life: Mark was Bishop of Arethusa in Syria. Under Constantine he destroyed a pagan temple and built a church; when Julian the Apostate came to power the pagans took revenge. Mark gave himself up, was beaten, plunged in sewers and hung in a basket smeared with honey to be stung by insects. He refused to pay for rebuilding the temple and was finally released. The deacon Cyril of Heliopolis was killed under Julian.

hypatius-gangra.life: Hypatius was Bishop of Gangra in Paphlagonia and took part in the First Ecumenical Council at Nicaea in 325. In 326, returning from Constantinople, he was attacked by followers of the Novatian schism and killed; he prayed for his murderers. Christians buried him, and his relics became known for healings. He was especially venerated in Russia, where the Ipatiev monastery at Kostroma bears his name.

titus-wonder-worker.life: Titus was a monk of the Studion monastery at Constantinople in the ninth century, known for strict fasting and gentleness. He was ordained hieromonk and was a spiritual father to many. He remained steadfast in defending the veneration of icons during the Iconoclast persecution. He was granted the gift of wonderworking and died in peace.

nicetas-medikion.life: Niketas was born in Bithynian Caesarea, entered the Medikion monastery under the abbot Nikephoros, was ordained a priest, and later became abbot. He had the gift of healing. Under Leo the Armenian he stood for the icons and was imprisoned. After a lapse he repented and again denounced Iconoclasm. He was imprisoned for six years and died in 824.

george-maleon.life: George lived in the ninth century and refused the marriage his parents arranged for him. He entered the monastery on Mount Maleon in the Peloponnesus, where many disciples gathered to him. He was known for clairvoyance and is said to have foreseen his own death three years before it came.

claudius-diodorus-victor-papias.life: Claudius, Diodorus, Victor, Papias and companions suffered at Corinth in 251 under Decius, according to the OCA entry for January 31. Victor and others were crushed under a stone pestle, Claudius's hands and feet were cut off, Diodorus was burned, and Papias was drowned. The OCA entry on this date says they are probably the same martyrs commemorated on January 31.

eutychios-patriarch-constantinople.life: Eutychius was born in Phrygia, became a monk and archimandrite in Amasea, and was made Patriarch of Constantinople in 552. He presided at the Fifth Ecumenical Council in 553. He opposed the Aphthartodocetist teaching favored by Justinian and was exiled in 565, returning in 577. He died in 582 on Thomas Sunday and was noted for healings and prophecy.

herodion-asyncritus-phlegon.life: Herodion, Asyncritus and Phlegon were counted among the Seventy Apostles sent out by Christ, and Paul names them in his Epistle to the Romans. According to the account read, Herodion was a kinsman and travelling companion of Paul and served as bishop of Patara, Asyncritus as bishop in Hyrcania, and Phlegon in Marathon in Thrace. They are said to have suffered greatly and to have won a martyr's crown.

eupsychios-caesarea.life: Eupsychios, born in Caesarea in Cappadocia, was a newly married Christian when, under Julian the Apostate, he tore down the city's temple of Fortuna. After giving his goods to the poor, he endured the rack and iron claws and was beheaded. The Christians of Caesarea later built a church over his grave, where healings were reported.

terence-pompeius-companions.life: Terence and forty companions were Christians of Africa who refused the sacrifice ordered by Decius, and the governor Fortunianus had thirty-six of them beheaded. Terence, Pompeius, Africanus and Maximus were kept in prison, where tradition holds they were fed by an angel and unharmed by snakes. They were afterward beheaded, and Christians buried their bodies outside the city.

antipas-pergamon.life: Antipas, a disciple of John the Theologian, was bishop of Pergamum. He is named as a faithful martyr in the Book of Revelation. After he turned many from pagan sacrifice, the priests are said to have put him inside a heated bronze bull at the temple of Artemis. Christians buried him, and he is invoked for toothache.

basil-bishop-parium.life: Basil, bishop of Parium, lived in the eighth century and was chosen bishop by the people who revered him as a true shepherd. When the iconoclast emperor Constantine V convened the Council of 754, he refused to sign its decree against icons and kept the heretics out of his diocese. He endured persecution, hunger and hardship, and stayed faithful to the Orthodox Church until his death.

martin-confessor-pope.life: Martin, a native of Tuscany, became Pope of Rome in 649 and convened the Lateran Council, which condemned Monothelitism. The emperor Constans II had him seized, held on Naxos, and tried in Constantinople on false charges. Sentenced to death, he was instead exiled to Cherson in the Crimea, where he died in 655 from illness and hardship. He is honored as a confessor.

aristarchus-pudens-trophimus.life: Aristarchus, Pudens and Trophimus were counted among the Seventy Apostles and appear in Acts and in Paul's epistles. Aristarchus, Paul's travelling companion, became bishop of Apamea in Syria. Pudens, a Roman senator, received Peter and Paul in his house, and is said to have been martyred under Nero. Trophimus, from Edessa, was Paul's disciple and companion.

symeon-bishop-persia.life: Symeon, bishop in Persia, was brought in chains before the emperor Sapor II after a tax on Christians was imposed, and was accused of siding with Rome. He refused to worship the sun. The priests Habdelai and Ananias and many others were beheaded in front of him, and Symeon was executed last. OCA gives the date as April 13, 344.

john-disciple-gregory-theologian.life: John, born at the end of the eighth century, became a disciple of Gregory of Decapolis and was tonsured by him at a monastery in Thessalonica. When the iconoclast persecution was renewed under Leo the Armenian, he went with Gregory and Joseph the Hymnographer to Constantinople, where they defended the veneration of icons. He died soon after Gregory, and Joseph moved their relics.

john-of-old-lavra.life: John lived in the eighth century in the Lavra of Saint Chariton, called the Old or Ancient Lavra, near Bethlehem and the Dead Sea. In his youth he left the world, venerated the holy places of Jerusalem and settled at the Lavra. He lived there in fasting, vigil and prayer, was ordained to the priesthood, and became known for his ascetic life.

januarius-bishop-beneventum.life: Januarius, bishop of Benevento, was arrested in Diocletian's persecution around 305. Tradition holds he came out of a furnace unharmed and that wild beasts in the arena would not touch him and his companions, the deacons Proculus, Sossius and Faustus, the reader Desiderius, and the laymen Eutychius and Acutius. The governor Menignus lost his sight and regained it through the bishop's prayer. They were afterward beheaded.

elizabeth-wonderworker.life: Elizabeth, from Constantinople, was dedicated to God from birth and was chosen abbess of the monastery of Saints Cosmas and Damian. She wore a hairshirt, kept strict fasts and received the gift of healing. Healings were reported at her tomb, and her relics were buried in the church of Saint George, where they remained incorrupt. OCA says her dates are uncertain.

basil-bishop-amasea.life: Basil became bishop of Amaseia in the fourth century and attended the councils of Ankyra and Neocaesarea in 314-315. Under Licinius he sheltered the maiden Glaphyra, who had fled the emperor, and he was summoned to Nikomedia. There he refused to sacrifice and was beheaded around 322. His body was recovered from the sea and buried in Amaseia.

simeon-bishop-jerusalem.life: Simeon, a kinsman of the Lord and son of Cleopas, succeeded James as bishop of Jerusalem. He is counted among the Seventy Apostles. He was denounced as a descendant of David and a Christian, and under the emperor Trajan was tortured and crucified. OCA gives the year as 107, when he was said to be over a hundred and twenty years old.

jason-sosipater.life: Jason of Tarsus and Sosipater of Patras were disciples of Paul, who calls them his kinsmen in Romans. Made bishops of Tarsus and Iconium, they traveled west and reached Corfu in the year 63, where they built a church, baptized many and were imprisoned. They won the governor's conversion and built more churches. They are said to have lived there into old age.

memnou-memnon-wonder-worker.life: Memnon lived from his youth in the Egyptian desert and became abbot of one of its monasteries, guiding the brothers with care. He was given the gift of clairvoyance. At his prayer a spring is said to have flowed in the wilderness and a plague of locusts perished. After his death, invoking his name was said to have saved shipwrecked sailors and to have driven off locusts.

prophet-jeremiah.life: Jeremiah, son of the priest Helkiah of Anathoth, was called to prophesy as a youth in about the seventh to sixth century B.C. He denounced Judah's idolatry and foretold the Babylonian conquest, and was thrown into a pit and imprisoned. After Jerusalem fell he mourned its ruin and was taken to Egypt. Tradition holds he was killed there by his own people.

timothy-maura-martyrs.life: Timothy, a reader in the Thebaid, and his wife Maura, married only twenty days, were arrested in Diocletian's persecution after he refused to surrender the church's books. He was blinded and tortured, and Maura was tormented and urged to deny Christ. Both stood firm, and the governor Arian had them crucified facing each other. They died on the tenth day, in 286.

pelagia-tarsus.life: Pelagia of Tarsus, daughter of pagan parents, came to faith and chose a life of virginity. She was baptized by Bishop Linus and refused to marry the emperor's adopted heir, and later Diocletian himself. Diocletian ordered her put into a heated bronze bull. Her bones are said to have been guarded by lions until Bishop Linus buried them.

hiob-righteous.life: Job, the righteous man of the land of Ausis, was blessed with wealth and children, then lost all and was struck with sores. He bore this with thanks to God. OCA says that God later restored his prosperity twofold and that he lived long afterward. The Church reads the Book of Job in Holy Week, seeing a parallel with Christ's suffering.

appearance-cross-jerusalem.life: This feast recalls the appearance of a luminous Cross in the sky over Jerusalem on the morning of May 7, 351, in the reign of Constantius. Reaching from Golgotha to the Mount of Olives, it was described by Patriarch Cyril of Jerusalem in a letter to the emperor, and Sozomen reports that it led many to the faith.

isaiah-prophet.life: Isaiah, of royal lineage, prophesied for about sixty years under the kings of Judah, beginning with a vision of the Lord surrounded by seraphim. His book foretells the captivity and return of the Jews and the coming of Christ, so he is called the Old Testament evangelist. By tradition he drew forth the spring of Siloam, and King Manasseh had him sawn in two.

epiphanius-cyprus.life: Epiphanius, born in Phoenicia, became a monk under Hilarion the Great and was consecrated bishop of Salamis in Cyprus in 367. He was known for his zeal for the faith, his almsgiving and his writings against heresies, notably the Panarion. He left a council against John Chrysostom, and died at sea in 403. The Seventh Ecumenical Council named him a Father of the Church.

germanus-constantinople.life: Germanus, born in Constantinople in the seventh century, became bishop of Cyzicus and then Patriarch of Constantinople. He opposed the iconoclasm of Leo III and was forced to resign after about fourteen years. He spent his last years in a monastery and died in about 740. He wrote on the liturgy and on icons, and the Seventh Council named him among the saints.

glyceria-martyr.life: Glyceria, from a prominent family, became a Christian in Trajanopolis in Thrace. When the prefect Sabinus ordered a sacrifice to Zeus, she is said to have entered the temple and prayed, and the idol fell and broke. She was imprisoned, tortured and miraculously preserved, and was killed by a lioness at Heraclea. OCA's account places her under the emperor Antoninus.

isidore-chios.life: Isidore, an Egyptian from Alexandria, was an officer in the Roman fleet during the reign of Decius when it anchored off Chios. A centurion denounced him as a Christian. He refused to sacrifice, was tortured, and was beheaded. The Christian Myrope buried his body and later died in prison. A chapel was built over their graves.

andronicus-junia-apostles.life: Andronicus and Junia, kinsmen and fellow prisoners of Paul, are named in Romans 16:7 as notable among the apostles. Andronicus became bishop of Pannonia, and the two preached in many lands, converting pagans and building churches. The church's service says they were martyred. Their relics were found near Constantinople in the fifth century, where a church was built over the place.

patrick-bishop-prusa.life: Patrick, bishop of Prusa in Bithynia, preached Christ openly and denounced pagan error. He and the priests Acacius, Menander and Polyainus were arrested and brought to the prefect Julius, who had Patrick thrown into a hot spring, where he was unharmed. All four were beheaded, around the year 100.

thallelaeus-martyr.life: Thallelaios was a young physician from Lebanon who was studying medicine when he was arrested at Aegae in Cilicia under Emperor Numerian. He confessed Christ before the prefect Theodore and survived attempted drowning and exposure to wild beasts before being beheaded, about 284. Because he treated the sick without payment, the Church counts him among the unmercenary physicians and invokes him for the sick.

basiliscus-comana.life: Basiliscus, a nephew of the Great Martyr Theodore the Recruit, was held in prison during the persecution under Maximian Galerius. On his way to Comana he was chained and made to wear nailed sandals; he was brought before the governor Agrippa and beheaded in 308. Christians buried him and later built a church over his relics, where healings were reported.

michael-bishop-synnada.life: Michael became a monk as a young man and was consecrated Bishop of Synnada in Phrygia by Patriarch Tarasius. He took part in the Seventh Ecumenical Council in 787. When Emperor Leo the Armenian renewed iconoclasm, Michael refused to remove icons from churches and was banished to Eudokiada, where he died about 821. He is venerated as a confessor of the holy icons.

simeon-stylites-junior.life: Simeon was born at Antioch and lost his father in an earthquake. As a boy he joined a monastery and lived on a pillar, later settling on the Wonderful Mountain near Antioch, where he founded a monastery. He was ordained priest and was known for healing and guidance. Sources differ on exact dates; he is said to have spent some sixty-eight years as a stylite, dying in the late sixth century.

carpos-alphaeus-apostles.life: Carpos was one of the Seventy Apostles sent out by Christ. He became a bishop in Macedonia (OCA says Verria; other calendar notes say Berea or Thrace) and is held to have died as a martyr. Tradition identifies him as the companion of Paul mentioned in Second Timothy, and records that he prayed for the salvation of sinners.

john-russian.life: John, born in Little Russia about 1690, served as a soldier under Peter I and was captured by Tatars in 1711 and taken to Asia Minor as a slave. He endured pressure to renounce Christianity, served his master faithfully, and lived in a stable, attending church at night. He died in 1730; his relics were found incorrupt, and are now at Evia in Greece.

nikita-bishop-chalcedon.life: Niketas became Bishop of Chalcedon and was known for charity toward the poor, orphans, widows and travelers. When Emperor Leo the Armenian attacked the holy icons, he spoke against iconoclasm, and he was tortured and sent into exile. He died in the early ninth century, and healings were reported at his relics.

theodosia-caesarea-cappadocia.life: Theodosia, a seventeen-year-old from Tyre, visited condemned Christians at the praetorium of Caesarea in Palestine and asked for their prayers. Arrested, she was tortured before the governor Urban, thrown into the sea, then exposed to wild beasts, and finally beheaded in 307 or 308. Tradition holds that she later appeared to her parents in glory.

isaakios-dalmatian.life: Isaac left the desert for Constantinople during the Arian persecution under Emperor Valens and warned the emperor to reopen the Orthodox churches. He was thrown into a ravine but survived, and Valens died in battle against the Goths. Under Theodosius the Great a monastery was built for him in the capital, which he led until his death in 383; it later took the name of his successor Dalmatos.

hermias-martyr.life: Hermias, an elderly soldier, was arrested at Comana in Cappadocia under Antoninus Pius and refused to sacrifice to idols before the governor Sebastian. He is said to have survived a red-hot oven, poison, boiling oil and other tortures, and healed some who had been blinded. He was finally beheaded, and healings occurred at his relics.

justin-martyr-philosopher.life: Born in Samaria to pagan Greek parents, Justin studied the Greek philosophies before turning to Christ and being baptized. He wrote two Apologies to defend Christians and the Dialogue with Trypho, and taught at Rome. After disputes with the philosopher Crescentius, he was arrested and beheaded with several companions about 165, before the prefect Rusticus.

nicephorus-patriarch-cp.life: Nikephoros was a court official who became a monk and, in 806, Patriarch of Constantinople. He defended the holy icons and wrote against iconoclasm. Emperor Leo the Armenian exiled him in 815 to Prokonnis, where he died in 828. In 846 his relics were returned to Constantinople, placed in Hagia Sophia for a day, and then enshrined in the Church of the Holy Apostles.

lucian-antioch-martyr.life: Lucillian, once a pagan priest, was baptized in old age under Emperor Aurelian and led many to Christ. Arrested at Nicomedia, he was tortured and imprisoned with four young men, Claudius, Hypatius, Paul and Dionysius. All survived a furnace, and at Byzantium the four were beheaded while Lucillian was crucified. The virgin Paula, who tended and buried the martyrs, was also beheaded.

metrophanes-cp.life: Metrophanes was the son of Dometius, bishop of Byzantium, and succeeded his brother Probus as bishop in 316. During the reign of Constantine the Great he is regarded as the first Patriarch of Constantinople. Too aged to attend the First Ecumenical Council in 325, he sent a representative, and the emperor and fathers visited him. He died soon after, in 326 by OCA's reckoning.

dorotheus-bishop-tyre.life: Dorotheus was Bishop of Tyre in Phoenicia under Diocletian, withdrew from the persecution, and returned to his see under Constantine the Great. In his old age he was arrested under Julian the Apostate at Udum on the Black Sea (modern Varna) and died under torture about 362, aged about 107. A collection of lives of prophets and apostles is attributed to him by some.

bessarion-egypt.life: Bessarion, an Egyptian, was baptized in youth, visited holy places and desert monasteries, and became a monk. He kept silence and ate only once a week, sometimes fasting forty days, and spent much of his life praying outdoors. He was granted the gift of wonderworking, which he used humbly and privately. He died peacefully in old age.

theodore-stratilates-translation.life: This day commemorates the transfer of the relics of the Great Martyr Theodore Stratelates, who was martyred at Heraklea on February 8, 319. He had asked his servant Varus to bury his body at his parents' estate at Euchaita, and the relics were moved on June 8. The day also recalls a miracle of his icon near Damascus, reported by Anastasius of Sinai and John of Damascus.

alexander-antonina-martyrs.life: Antonina, a Christian virgin from Asia Minor, was tortured before the governor Festus and imprisoned. A soldier named Alexander helped her escape by giving her his military cloak, and he was punished in her place. Antonina then came forward voluntarily, and both were tortured and burned in 313. Their relics were taken to Constantinople. The governor died in torment after seven days.

aquilina-byblos.life: Aquilina was a Christian girl of Byblos in Phoenicia who was twelve by OCA's account (Orthocal says ten to twelve) when she persuaded a friend to convert. She was denounced and tortured before the governor Volusian under Diocletian and left for dead, but appeared before him again and was beheaded in 293. Her relics were later taken to Constantinople and healed the sick.

elisha-prophet.life: Elisha, from near the Jordan, was called by the prophet Elijah and received a double portion of his spirit when Elijah was taken up in a fiery chariot. He served more than sixty-five years under six kings of Israel and worked miracles, healing Naaman and raising the Shunamite woman's son. He died in old age at Samaria; a dead man touched his bones and revived.

augustine-hippo.life: Augustine was born at Thagaste in North Africa, raised by his mother Monica, and taught rhetoric before being baptized at Milan under Ambrose. Ordained priest at Hippo in 391, he later became its bishop for about thirty-five years and wrote against the Donatists, Manichaeans and Pelagians, as well as The City of God and the Confessions. He died in 430; the Orthodox Church keeps his memory on June 15.

tikhon-amathous.life: Tikhon was born at Amathus on Cyprus, where as a young man he gave bread from his father's bakery to the poor. Ordained and chosen bishop of Amathus, he was consecrated by Epiphanius of Cyprus, and he worked against paganism there. He planted vine cuttings that bore fruit used for Eucharistic wine. OCA places his death in 425.

manuel-sabel-ismael.life: Manuel, Sabel and Ismael were brothers from a Persian family, raised as Christians by their mother. Sent by the Persian king as envoys to Emperor Julian the Apostate, they refused to join in pagan sacrifice and were tortured and beheaded in 362. Their bodies are said to have been swallowed by the earth and then restored to Christians, who buried them.

leontius-martyr.life: Leontius was a Greek officer at Tripoli in Phoenicia under Vespasian. Hypatius and Theodulus were sent to arrest him, but were converted and baptized, and were beheaded by the governor Adrian. Leontius refused to renounce Christ and was tortured to death. The three are commemorated together.

methodius-bishop-patara.life: Methodius, bishop of Patara in Lycia, was known for his humility and for defending Orthodoxy against paganism and the Origenist heresy. He left writings explaining doctrine and Scripture. Arrested by pagans, he confessed Christ and was beheaded in 312. Sources differ on his see and place of death, some naming Olympus or Tyre.

julian-tarsus-martyr.life: Julian, born in Cilicia to a pagan senator and a Christian mother, was baptized at Tarsus. At eighteen he was arrested under Diocletian and was led through the cities of Cilicia for a year of torture. His mother encouraged him to stand firm and was herself punished. He was sewn into a sack with snakes and sand and thrown into the sea; his body was buried at Alexandria and later moved to Antioch.

agrippina-rome-martyr.life: Agrippina was a Roman virgin who, under Emperor Valerian, presented herself before the court as a Christian. She was beaten so severely that she died of her injuries. Bassa, Paula and Agathonike took her body to Sicily, where miracles were reported at her grave, and in the eleventh century her relics were moved to Constantinople.

febronia-nisibis.life: Febronia was raised in a convent under her aunt, the abbess Bryaine, in the time of Diocletian. When the officer Selinus came to destroy Christians, she refused to deny Christ and was tortured, mutilated and beheaded. Her companion Thomais recorded her martyrdom, and Hieria, whom she had taught, accepted baptism. Relics were placed at Nisibis by Bishop James and later at Constantinople.

david-thessalonica.life: David of Thessalonica lived the ascetic life at the monastery of Saints Theodore and Mercurius, and for three years dwelt in an almond tree in prayer until an angel told him to come down. He was given the gift of healing and counseled many visitors. He once carried hot coals in his hands without harm. He died about 540.

sampson-hospitable.life: Sampson was born in Rome, studied medicine, and turned his family estate into a clinic for the sick. He went to Constantinople, where Patriarch Menas ordained him priest, and he healed Emperor Justinian, who then built a hospice at his request. He died in 530 and was buried at the church of Saint Mokios. OCA notes that Procopius places the hospice earlier.

cosmas-damian-rome.life: Cosmas and Damian were brothers and physicians born in Rome. They treated the sick without payment, telling patients that healing came from Christ, and so became known as unmercenary physicians. Tradition holds that they healed a persecuting emperor of blindness and were released. Later their former teacher, envious of their fame, led them into the hills and killed them. They are distinguished from the pairs of the same name in Asia Minor and Arabia.

hyacinth-caesarea.life: Hyacinth, a young Christian from Caesarea in Cappadocia, served as a chamberlain at the court of the emperor Trajan. A servant reported that he prayed to Christ instead of honoring the idols. Brought before Trajan, he confessed his faith, was whipped and imprisoned, and refused food offered to idols. He died in prison, and his relics were later taken to Caesarea.
