andrew-crete-bishop.life: Andrew was born in Damascus, became a monk at the monastery of St Sabbas near Jerusalem, and served the Jerusalem Patriarchate. He took part in the Sixth Ecumenical Council, served in Constantinople as a deacon, and became archbishop of Crete. A hymnographer, he composed the Great Canon of Repentance sung in Lent. He died returning to Crete, around 712 to 740 according to differing accounts.

athanasios-athos.life: Athanasius, born in Trebizond, studied in Constantinople and became a monk under Michael Maleinos. Settling on Mount Athos, he founded the Great Lavra with support from Nikephoros Phocas and gave it a communal rule. Tradition holds that the Mother of God appeared to him and a spring flowed from a rock. He died c. 1003 when part of the church under construction collapsed.

sisoes-great.life: Sisoes the Great was an Egyptian desert monk who lived in the cave once used by Anthony the Great and spent some sixty years in ascetic labor. Known for humility and mercy toward visitors, he was said to have gifts of healing. His sayings stress regarding oneself as lower than others. At his death, according to the account, his face shone and he said he had barely begun to repent.

placing-robe-lord-moscow.life: This feast marks the arrival and placing of a part of the Lord's robe in the Dormition cathedral in Moscow in 1625. The relic had been kept in Georgia and was carried off by the Persian shah Abbas I, who sent it to Tsar Michael and Patriarch Philaret. Its authenticity was attested by hierarchs, and it is brought out for veneration each July 10.

proclus-hilary-martyrs.life: Proclus and his nephew Hilary (Hilarion) were Christians from the village of Kallippi near Ancyra who suffered in the persecution under Trajan. Proclus confessed Christ before the governor, was tortured, and died shot with arrows. Hilary, meeting his uncle on the way to execution, declared himself a Christian and was beheaded three days later. They were buried in a single grave.

gabriel-archangel-july.life: This synaxis honors the Archangel Gabriel and the revelations and acts attributed to him in Scripture and afterward. It repeats the synaxis kept on March 26, the day after the Annunciation. It was instituted in the ninth century, perhaps for the dedication of a church in Constantinople, and was originally kept on October 16.

emilian-dorystolon.life: Emilian, a slave and secret Christian in Dorostolon on the Danube, lived under Julian the Apostate. After the imperial edict against Christians, he smashed idols in a pagan temple and, when an innocent man was beaten for it, declared himself guilty. Brought before the governor, he refused to deny Christ and was burned alive. His relics were later taken to Constantinople.

macrina-sister-basil.life: Macrina was the elder sister of Basil the Great and Gregory of Nyssa, born in Cappadocia. After her betrothed died, she chose a life of virginity and helped raise her younger brothers. She persuaded her mother Emilia to join her in a women's monastery, which she led after Emilia's death. Gregory wrote of her holiness. She died in the late fourth century.

symeon-fool-for-christ.life: Symeon and John were close friends from Edessa who, after a pilgrimage to Jerusalem, became monks and lived in the desert near the Jordan and Dead Sea for many years. Symeon then left to serve others in Emesa in Syria, hiding his holiness by feigning madness. John stayed in the desert. Symeon died around 590, and John soon afterward.

christina-tire-martyr.life: Christina was the daughter of Urban, governor of Tyre, who kept her in a house with idols. Coming to faith in Christ, she smashed the idols. Her father had her tortured, and sources report she survived several ordeals before being put to the sword under a later governor. Her father died, and many came to believe through her witness. She is remembered as a martyr of the third century.

hermolaus-hieromartyr.life: Hermolaus was a priest of Nicomedia who survived the persecution of 303 and baptized the young Pantoleon, later the great martyr Panteleimon. He and the priests Hermippus and Hermocrates were arrested when Panteleimon was tried. They refused to sacrifice to idols and, after Hermolaus was told in a vision of his coming death, were beheaded around 305.

prochorus-nicanor-timon-parmenas.life: Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon and Parmenas were four of the seven men chosen as deacons in Acts 6. They are also counted among the Seventy apostles. Prochorus became bishop of Nicomedia and is said to have accompanied John to Patmos. Timon became bishop of Bostra, and Parmenas preached in Macedonia. Nicanor is also commemorated December 28, and they died at different times and places.

callinicos-martyr.life: Callinicus, a native of Cilicia, traveled through cities preaching Christ to pagans. Arrested in Ancyra and tortured by the governor Sacerdonus, he was driven in nail-studded sandals toward Gangra. On the way he is said to have caused water to flow from a rock for thirsty soldiers. At Gangra he was burned in a fire, and believers buried his unharmed body.

silas-apostle.life: Silas, one of the Seventy, was a leading man in the Jerusalem church and was sent with Paul and Barnabas to Antioch with the decision of the Apostolic Council. He then joined Paul's missions in Syria, Cilicia and Macedonia and was imprisoned with him at Philippi. He became bishop of Corinth and died there; he is commemorated with Silvanus, Crescens, Epenetus and Andronicus.

joseph-of-arimathea-nicodemus.life: Joseph of Arimathea was a wealthy member of the Sanhedrin and a secret disciple of Jesus. After the Crucifixion he asked Pilate for the body and, with Nicodemus, laid it in his own new tomb. He is said to have preached the Gospel in many lands, and one tradition holds that he died in England. Nicodemus's relics are marked on August 2.

translation-stephen-protomartyr.life: This feast commemorates the translation of the relics of the first martyr and archdeacon Stephen. After his stoning, Gamaliel buried him near Jerusalem, and his relics were found in 415. Under Theodosius the Younger they were taken from Jerusalem to Constantinople, about 428, and on August 2 were placed in a church built in his name.

isaakios-dalmatos-faustus.life: Isaac, Dalmatus and Faustus are the founding fathers of the Dalmatian Monastery in Constantinople. Isaac, a former soldier, defied the Arian emperor Valens and became the monastery's first abbot. Dalmatus, an army officer, entered it with his son Faustus, succeeded Isaac, and defended the faith at the Council of Ephesus in 431. Faustus later succeeded his father as abbot.

seven-sleepers-ephesus.life: Seven young Christians of Ephesus, soldiers according to the account, hid from the persecution under Decius in a cave, which was sealed. Tradition holds that God put them into a sleep of nearly two centuries. In the reign of Theodosius the Younger they woke and were found, and their story served against a heresy denying the resurrection of the dead. They then died peacefully.

forefeast-transfiguration.life: The forefeast prepares for the Transfiguration of the Lord on August 6, when Christ took Peter, James and John up Mount Tabor and was transfigured before them. His face shone like light, and Moses and Elijah appeared with Him. The Church observes the day as an anticipation of that event.

dometius-persia.life: Dometius was born in Persia, converted to Christianity as a youth, and became a monk near Nisibis. He later lived in a monastery at Theodosiopolis, was ordained deacon, and withdrew to a mountain in Syria, where many came for healing. When Julian the Apostate passed through in 363, he had Dometius and his two disciples walled up in a cave.

emilian-bishop-cyzicus.life: Emilian was bishop of Cyzicus from 787 to 815. Under the iconoclast emperor Leo the Armenian he was summoned with other bishops and told the emperor that the question of icons belonged to the Church, not the court. He was banished in 815 and suffered in exile until his death in 820. He is honored as a confessor for defending the veneration of icons.

lawrence-archdeacon-rome.life: Lawrence was archdeacon of the Church of Rome under the emperor Valerian. When Pope Sixtus was arrested, Lawrence distributed the Church's treasures to the poor. Asked to give up the treasures, he presented the poor and needy instead. He was tortured and died on a red-hot gridiron on August 10, 258, and is buried at Rome.

euplus-catania-deacon.life: Euplus was an archdeacon in Catania, Sicily, who carried the Gospel with him and preached to the pagans. Arrested under Diocletian and Maximian, he was tortured and imprisoned, and confessed Christ a second time before the governor Calvisianus. Led to execution with the Gospel hung around his neck, he read to the crowd, and was beheaded in 304.

maximus-confessor-repose.life: Maximus the Confessor, born in Constantinople about 580, served as secretary to Emperor Heraclius before becoming a monk. He opposed Monothelitism, taught in Africa and Rome, and was arrested under Constans II. His tongue and right hand were cut off and he was exiled to Lazika, where he died in 662. OCA marks August 13 as the translation of his relics.

forefeast-dormition.life: The forefeast of the Dormition begins the celebration of the Virgin Mary's falling asleep on August 15. OCA notes that the troparion of the forefeast invites the faithful to gather in gladness because the Theotokos is about to depart from earth to heaven.

myron-martyr-cyzicus.life: Myron was a presbyter in Achaia who was arrested while celebrating the Liturgy on Christmas under the emperor Decius. He pleaded for his flock and was tortured, and in the account survived fire and wild beasts. The governor Antipater took his own life. Myron was taken to Cyzicus and beheaded around 250.

floros-lavros-martyrs.life: Florus and Laurus were brothers and stonemasons in Illyria who were set to build a pagan temple. When a stone splinter injured the eye of the pagan priest's son, they prayed and he was healed, and the priest's family came to faith. After finishing the building they set a cross in it and kept vigil; the governor then had them thrown into a well and covered with earth. Their relics were later taken to Constantinople.

andrew-stratelates.life: Andrew was a Syrian officer in the Roman army, called stratelates ("commander") after he led a small force to victory over the Persians. Denounced as a Christian at Antioch, he was tortured and then released. He withdrew with 2,593 soldiers to Tarsus, where Bishop Peter baptized them. Overtaken in the Taurus mountains, all were beheaded; a healing spring is said to have appeared where their blood flowed.

samuel-prophet.life: Samuel was the last of the Judges of Israel. When the people demanded a king he anointed Saul, later rebuked Saul for disobedience, and anointed David, whom he had sheltered from Saul. His story is told in the First Book of Samuel, and he died at a great age. The Church records that his relics were moved from Judea to Constantinople in 406.

thaddaeus-apostle.life: Thaddaeus, one of the Seventy Apostles, was a Jew of Edessa and is distinguished from the Thaddaeus among the Twelve. After Christ's Resurrection he preached in Syria and Mesopotamia, instructed and baptized King Abgar of Edessa, and established churches. Sources differ on his end: OCA gives a peaceful death at Beirut (or Edessa), while another account says he was martyred.

agathonikos-martyr.life: Agathonikos lived in Nicomedia, where he turned many pagans to faith in Christ. For this he and several companions were seized, beaten and taken toward Byzantium; some died of their treatment on the way. The survivors were tried before the emperor and beheaded at Selymbria in Thrace. His relics later rested in a church bearing his name at Constantinople.

leavetaking-dormition.life: The Church concludes its celebration of the Dormition of the Theotokos on this day. The service of the feast is sung again, leaving out the entrance, readings and litya at Vespers, and the polyeleos and Gospel at Matins. On Mount Athos the feast is prolonged to August 28.

eutyches-hieromartyr.life: Eutyches, a native of Sebaste in Palestine, was a disciple of John the Theologian and of Paul, and was made a bishop by the apostles. Though not one of the Seventy, he is called an apostle for his labors. He travelled widely preaching the Gospel and endured imprisonment and torture. Accounts of his death differ, and he is honored as a hieromartyr.

pimen-great.life: Pimen the Great was an Egyptian ascetic of the fourth and fifth centuries. He entered a monastery with his brothers Anoub and Paisius, and the three lived in strict silence and labor. He became a trusted spiritual guide, and his answers to monks were written down; many appear in the Sayings of the Desert Fathers. He died in peace at a great age.

moses-prophet-ethiopia.life: Moses the Ethiopian was a slave in Egypt who, after a murder, was driven out by his master and became leader of a band of robbers. He repented and entered a desert monastery, where he lived by fasting and prayer under the guidance of Isidore. He grew renowned for humility and wisdom. In old age he refused to flee attacking raiders and was killed with six other monks.

alexander-john-paul-cp-patriarchs.life: Three Patriarchs of Constantinople are remembered together. Alexander represented the ailing Patriarch Metrophanes at the First Ecumenical Council, succeeded him, and opposed Arius; he died about 340. John (the Faster, reposed 595, by one account) was known for his ascetic life and a penitential guide for confessors. Paul the New governed for five years before resigning to take the Great Schema.

indiction-new-year.life: September 1 marks the beginning of the Church year, called the Indiction. Tradition links it to Christ's reading from Isaiah in the synagogue at Nazareth, and the First Ecumenical Council fixed it as the Church's New Year. The day also honors Symeon the Stylite the Elder, who lived as a monk and then prayed on tall pillars, drawing many pilgrims; he died in 459.

mamas-martyr.life: Mamas was born to Christian parents, Theodotus and Rufina, who died in prison for their faith; a widow named Ammia raised him. Arrested as a boy of fifteen, he refused to deny Christ even before Emperor Aurelian. He escaped torture and lived in solitude near Caesarea in Cappadocia, where tradition says wild animals befriended him. He was eventually found and stabbed with a trident.

anthimos-bishop-nicomedia.life: Anthimos was bishop of Nicomedia during the persecution under Diocletian and Maximian, after twenty thousand Christians there were put to death. He hid in a village to care for his flock. When soldiers came, he welcomed and fed them, and they were moved by his kindness and by his words, and some were baptized. After steadfastly confessing Christ before Maximian, he was beheaded in about 303 or 304.

phoebe-deaconess-cenchreae.life: Phoebe was a deaconess of the church at Cenchreae, the harbor village of Corinth. The Apostle Paul commends her in Romans 16:1-2 as a helper of many, including himself, and asks that she be received in the Lord. She may have carried his Epistle to the Romans and then continued her service in Rome. Beyond Scripture, little is recorded about her.

babylas-bishop-antioch.life: Babylas was bishop of Antioch under the emperor Decius, who came to the city and was barred from entering the church by the bishop. Babylas was imprisoned and compelled to watch the beheading of three young men, Urban, Prilidian and Epolonius, and their mother Christodoula; he was then beheaded. Years later, when Julian the Apostate had his relics removed from Daphne, the nearby shrine of Apollo was destroyed.

zacharias-prophet-elizabeth.life: Zacharias was a priest of the line of Aaron, and Elizabeth his wife, who was a relative of the Virgin Mary's mother Anna. Luke's Gospel tells how an angel announced to the aged, childless couple that they would have a son, John the Baptist. A traditional account says Zacharias was later put to death in the Temple after declaring the virginity of Mary.

forefeast-nativity-theotokos.life: The Forefeast prepares for the Nativity of the Theotokos on September 8. At Great Vespers three Old Testament readings are read: Jacob's ladder, the closed gate of the sanctuary in Ezekiel, and Wisdom's house in Proverbs. The Church interprets these as foreshadowing the Mother of God.

joachim-anna-parents-theotokos.life: Joachim, of the tribe of Judah, and Anna, daughter of the priest Matthan, were the parents of the Theotokos. They lived at Nazareth and were childless into old age, which brought them scorn. Tradition holds that an angel told each of them that they would have a daughter. They are said to have died in peace soon after she was taken to live in the Temple.

menodora-metrodora-nymphodora.life: Menodora, Metrodora and Nymphodora were sisters from Bithynia who withdrew to a mountain to live in prayer, fasting and labor. Healings through their prayers made them known, and the governor had them arrested. When they refused his flattery and demands to renounce Christ, he had them tortured to death, Menodora first. Christians afterward buried their bodies.

theodora-alexandria.life: Theodora, a married woman of Alexandria, fell into adultery and was struck with remorse. Dressed as a man and calling herself Theodore, she entered a men's monastery, where her fasting, prayer and tears impressed the brothers. Her identity was discovered only after her death. Her husband came to her funeral and afterward lived in her former cell. She is also said to have healed the sick.

autonomus-bishop-martyr.life: Autonomus was a bishop in Italy who left during Diocletian's persecution and settled in Bithynia. There he converted many pagans and consecrated a church of the Archangel Michael. When new converts destroyed a pagan temple, pagans attacked the church during the Liturgy and killed him at the altar. A church was later built over his tomb.

forefeast-exaltation-cross.life: This is the one-day Forefeast of the Exaltation of the Cross, which is followed by seven days of afterfeast. The day also commemorates the consecration in 335 of the Church of the Resurrection on Golgotha in Jerusalem, built by Constantine the Great and his mother Helen. Bishop Makarios of Jerusalem presided and also lifted up the Cross for the people.

niketas-goth-martyr.life: Niketas was a Goth from the Danube region, baptized by Bishop Theophilos of the Goths, who had attended the First Ecumenical Council. He taught many of his people the faith. When the pagan ruler Athanaric renewed his persecution of Christians, Niketas was tortured and burned to death, and his body was found unharmed. His friend Marianus took the relics to Mopsuestia in Cilicia.

sophia-vera-nadezda-lyubov.life: Sophia was a widow who raised her three daughters, Faith, Hope and Love, aged twelve, ten and nine. During the reign of Hadrian, the four were brought before the authorities and ordered to sacrifice to the goddess Artemis. The girls refused and were tortured and executed before their mother. She buried them, mourned for three days at their grave, and died in peace, and is counted among the martyrs.

eumenios-bishop-gortyna.life: Eumenios gave his possessions to the poor in youth and was chosen bishop of Gortyna on Crete. He cared for the poor and sorrowing and is credited with many miracles, including healing the sick and bringing rain in a drought. He defended Orthodoxy against the Monophysites and, per OCA, was exiled to the Thebaid in Egypt, where he died in the seventh century. His body was later buried at Gortyna.

trophimos-sabbatios-dorymedon.life: Trophimos and Sabbatios came to Antioch during a pagan festival and declared themselves Christians. Sabbatios died under torture, and Trophimos was sent to Synnada for further torments. Dorymedon, an official there, pitied him and visited him in prison. When Dorymedon refused to worship idols and confessed Christ, he and Trophimos were tortured, exposed to wild beasts, and beheaded under Probus.

quadratus-prophet.life: Quadratus was one of the Seventy Apostles appointed by Christ. He preached in Athens and Magnesia and served as bishop of Athens. Pagans stoned him and then imprisoned him, where he died of starvation; he was buried at Magnesia. Tradition holds that his defense of the faith, presented to Emperor Hadrian, led to easing the persecution of Christians.

phocas-gardener-sinope.life: Phocas of Sinope lived by tending a garden near the Black Sea, giving whatever he earned to the poor. He welcomed soldiers sent to arrest him as guests, and when they disclosed their mission, he prepared his own grave and told them who he was. They beheaded him. A church was built at the site, and sailors invoke him for protection at sea.

conception-john-baptist.life: The Church celebrates the conception of John the Baptist by Elizabeth, the wife of the priest Zacharias, as told in Luke 1. An angel announced to the aged, childless Zacharias in the Temple that he would have a son who would go before the Messiah. The feast marks God's mercy to the righteous couple and the beginning of the Forerunner's life.

euphrosyne-alexandria.life: Euphrosyne was the only daughter of the wealthy Paphnutios of Alexandria. Unwilling to marry, she left home and entered a men's monastery disguised as a man, taking the name Smaragdos. She lived there as an ascetic for thirty-eight years and revealed her identity only on her deathbed. Her father later became a monk in the same monastery and died ten years after her.

callistratos-companions.life: Callistratos, a Christian soldier from Carthage, was reported for praying at night. He refused to sacrifice to idols and was beaten, then sewn into a sack and thrown into the sea, from which he emerged unharmed. Forty-nine fellow soldiers confessed Christ at this sight. Callistratos taught them in prison, and all were beheaded, in 288 or 304 according to differing sources.

chariton-confessor.life: Chariton was a native of Iconium who was tortured as a Christian under Emperor Aurelian but survived. On pilgrimage to Jerusalem he was seized by robbers; after his rescue from the cave where they held him, he settled there as an ascetic. He founded Pharan, a monastery near Jericho, and Souka, drawing many disciples, and died about 350. He is regarded as a pioneer of monastic life in the Judean wilderness.

cyriacus-hermit.life: Kyriakos (Cyriacus) was born in Corinth and went to Palestine in his youth, becoming a monk under Saint Euthymios the Great and training with Saint Gerasimos. He spent three decades in Saint Chariton's monastery at Souka, then lived in desert retreats where he healed the sick. He defended Orthodox teaching against Origenism and died at the age of 109.

cyprian-ustyna-martyrs.life: Tradition holds that Cyprian of Antioch was a pagan sorcerer who turned to Christ after his spells failed against the prayer and fasting of the young Christian Justina. Baptized, he became a bishop, and Justina led a convent. Arrested in Diocletian's persecution, both were taken to Nicomedia and beheaded in 304, together with a soldier named Theoktistos.

dionysius-areopagite.life: Dionysius was a member of the Athenian Areopagus who became a Christian after hearing Saint Paul preach there (Acts 17:34). Tradition holds that Paul made him bishop of Athens and that he later preached in the West, being beheaded in Gaul with Rusticus and Eleutherius. Writings on the heavenly and church hierarchies, the divine names and mystical theology are traditionally ascribed to him.

hierotheos-bishop-athens.life: Hierotheos, a judge of the Athenian Areopagus, became a Christian through the Apostle Paul, as did Dionysius the Areopagite. Paul consecrated him a bishop, and he is counted as the first bishop of Athens. Tradition holds that he and Dionysius attended the burial of the Theotokos. He is said to have died as a martyr in the first century.

charitina-martyr.life: Charitina came from Amisos in Pontus and, in the reign of Diocletian, served in the household of the Roman Christian Claudius, who raised her like a daughter. Brought before a governor for leading others to Christ, she endured many tortures, including being cast into the sea, from which she emerged unharmed. She died praying, in 304, and Claudius buried her body.

sergios-bacchus.life: Sergios and Bacchus were officers in the Roman army in Syria, trusted by the emperor until he learned they were Christians. They refused to sacrifice to idols, were stripped of rank and paraded in women's clothing, then sent to a governor. Bacchus died under a beating; Sergios, made to walk in iron shoes studded with nails, was beheaded. They became widely venerated soldier-martyrs.

pelagia-penitent.life: Pelagia was a celebrated dancer and courtesan of Antioch who, after hearing the preaching of Bishop Nonnus, repented and was baptized by him. She gave her wealth to the poor, travelled to Jerusalem, and lived on the Mount of Olives disguised as a monk named Pelagius. Her burial took place in that same cell. The Church remembers her as a model of repentance.

eulampios-eulampia.life: Eulampios and his sister Eulampia lived at Nicomedia in the early fourth century. When Eulampios was tried for his faith, tradition holds that he toppled a pagan idol in Christ's name, and Eulampia then declared herself a Christian too. Eulampios was beheaded and Eulampia died of her torments. About two hundred who were converted by the miracles were also put to death.

philip-apostle-october.life: Philip was one of the Seven chosen at Jerusalem to oversee care for the poor and widows, and is also counted among the Seventy. After Stephen's martyrdom he preached in Samaria and, on the road to Gaza, baptized an Ethiopian official (Acts 8). He is distinct from Philip of the Twelve, who is commemorated on November 14.

euthymios-thessalonica.life: Euthymios, born Nicetas at Ancyra in Galatia, left his wife and daughter for monastic life, first on Mount Olympus and then on Mount Athos, where he lived for years in silence in a cave. He later lived as a stylite near Thessalonica and founded two monasteries on Mount Peristeros, where his wife and mother became nuns. He died on the island of Hiera in 898, and his relics were taken to Thessalonica.

longinus-centurion.life: Longinus was the Roman centurion at the Crucifixion who confessed that Jesus was the Son of God, and tradition identifies him as the soldier who pierced Christ's side. After baptism he left the army and preached in Cappadocia, where he and two companions were beheaded by soldiers sent from Pilate. According to tradition, a blind widow later recovered his head and regained her sight.

hosea-prophet.life: Hosea, first of the minor prophets, served in the northern kingdom of Israel for more than sixty years. He denounced idolatry and foretold captivity at Assyrian hands. His book speaks of the end of the old sacrifices and, in Christian reading, points to Christ's return from Egypt and victory over death. Sources place him in the ninth or eighth century before Christ.

artemios-antioch-martyr.life: Artemios was a senior Roman commander under Constantine and Constantius and was made governor of Egypt. He carried the relics of the apostles Andrew and Luke to Constantinople. At Antioch he openly rebuked Emperor Julian the Apostate for persecuting Christians, was tortured and beheaded, around 362. His relics were taken to Constantinople, and he is invoked by those suffering hernias.

hilarion-great.life: Hilarion was born about 291 near Gaza to pagan parents, was baptized in Alexandria, and visited Anthony the Great. After giving away his inheritance he lived as a hermit in the desert, where his healing gifts drew disciples, and monasteries arose across Palestine under his guidance. He is regarded as the founder of Palestinian monasticism. He spent his last years on Cyprus and died about 371.

abercius-bishop-hieropolis.life: Averkios (Abercius) was bishop of Hieropolis in Phrygia in the second century, in a largely pagan city. At an angel's command he destroyed its idols, healed the possessed and baptized many townspeople, then preached through Syria, Cilicia and Mesopotamia and visited Rome. For these labors he is called Equal-to-the-Apostles. The epitaph he composed for his tomb survives in the Lateran Museum. He died about 167.

arethas-martyrs-nagran.life: Arethas governed Najran, a Christian city in Arabia. In 523 the Jewish king Dunaan besieged it and, after swearing to spare the people, seized it by trickery and had the clergy burned. Arethas and, by the Orthodox account, over four thousand Christians died for refusing to deny Christ. Their sufferings are commemorated together.

martyrs-notarios.life: Marcian, a reader, and Martyrios, a subdeacon, served as notaries to Patriarch Paul the Confessor of Constantinople. After Arians seized the see and killed Paul, the two refused offers of gold and high office to join them. For confessing Orthodoxy they were beheaded in the mid-fourth century. Their relics were later moved to a church dedicated to them, where healings were reported.

nestor-martyr-thessalonica.life: Nestor was a young Christian of Thessalonica who had been taught the faith by Saint Demetrios. When Emperor Maximian's giant champion Lyaios was killing Christians in staged combats, Nestor sought Demetrios's blessing, faced him, and threw him onto the spears below the platform. Enraged, Maximian had Nestor beheaded and Demetrios speared.

terence-neonilla-family.life: Terence, a Syrian, his spouse Neonila and seven children were denounced as Christians and questioned by the authorities. They confessed Christ and endured torments while encouraging one another. Tradition holds that angels freed them from their bonds, wild beasts did not harm them, and a cauldron of boiling pitch spared them, after which they were beheaded.
terence-neonilla-family.period: date not given in source (Roman persecution era)

stephen-sabaite-hymnographer.life: Stephen lived as a monk at the Lavra of Saint Sabas in Palestine for many decades. With Andrew the Blind he was among the first to compose idiomela, the hymns sung from the Sunday of the Publican and Pharisee to Palm Sunday. A nephew of Saint John of Damascus, he was born near Gaza and died at the lavra in the late eighth or early ninth century.

anastasia-rome.life: Anastasia lost her parents at three and was raised in a women's monastery by the abbess Sophia, becoming known for her asceticism. During the persecution under Decius, the city administrator Probus had her arrested and tortured when she refused to renounce Christ. She was beheaded, and Sophia, guided by an angel, found and buried her body. She is called a monastic martyr.

zenobius-zenobia.life: Zenobios, bishop of Aegae in Cilicia, and his sister Zenobia were raised Christian and gave their inheritance to the poor. Zenobios, gifted with healing, was chosen bishop. When Diocletian's persecution began he was the first arrested; the governor Licius had him crucified and tortured, and Zenobia, confessing her own faith, shared his sufferings. Both were beheaded and buried by the priest Hermogenes.

stachys-amplias-urban-apostles.life: These six are counted among the Seventy Apostles. Tradition holds that Stachys became bishop of Byzantium, Amplias bishop of Diopolis, Urban bishop of Macedonia, Narcissus bishop of Athens, and Apelles bishop of Herakleia, while Aristobulus, brother of Barnabas, preached in Britain. Stachys and Aristobulus died in peace, whereas Amplias, Urban and Narcissus were killed for opposing idol worship.
stachys-amplias-urban-apostles.place: Byzantium; Diopolis; Macedonia; Athens; Herakleia; Britain

acindynus-pegasius-anempodistus.life: Acindynus, Pegasius, Anempodistus, Elpidephoros and Aphthonius were secret Christians among the courtiers of King Sapor II of Persia. Denounced in his persecution, they confessed the Holy Trinity before the king. Elpidephoros died in a massacre of about seven thousand Christians who accompanied the procession; Acindynus, Pegasius and Anempodistus were burned, and Christians buried their unharmed bodies.

acepsimas-bishop-persia.life: Acepsimas, an eighty-year-old bishop of Naesson in Persia, was arrested when King Sapor ordered Christian clergy hunted down. Taken to Arbela, he was beaten and jailed, and Joseph, a presbyter, and Aeithalas, a deacon, were later jailed with him. After three years they refused to worship Sapor's gods. Acepsimas was beheaded, while Joseph and Aeithalas were stoned.

galacteon-episteme.life: Galacteon was the son of Kletophon and Leukippe of Emesa in Syria, born after Leukippe was baptized by the old priest Onuphrios. He chose monastic life, converted and baptized his betrothed Episteme, and they withdrew to Mount Publion. When soldiers came they were arrested and, after terrible torments, beheaded. Their servant Eutolmius buried them and later wrote their story.

thirty-three-martyrs-melitene.life: Hieron, a Cappadocian from Tiana, was a strong man whom the commander Lysias tried to conscript during the persecution under Diocletian and Maximian. He refused to serve persecutors, but later submitted at a friend's urging. At Melitene he and thirty-two other soldiers refused to sacrifice to idols and, after tortures, were beheaded. A Christian named Chrysanthus later built a church there.

menas-victor-vincent.life: On 11 November the Church remembers Menas, an Egyptian soldier who left the army during the persecution under Diocletian and Maximian, confessed Christ publicly in Phrygia and was beheaded in 304. It also remembers Victor, a soldier martyred at Damascus under Marcus Aurelius, and Vincent, a deacon of Saragossa, who died in 304 after fierce tortures under the governor Dacian.

plato-roman.life: Platon, born at Ancyra in Galatia, was the brother of the martyr Antiochus the Physician. As a young man he travelled through cities preaching the Gospel to pagans. Arrested and brought before the governor Agrippinus, he refused both flattery and threats, endured torture and imprisonment, and would not honor the pagan gods. He was then beheaded.

abdias-prophet.life: Obadiah, the fourth of the Twelve Minor Prophets, lived in the ninth century B.C. and served as steward to King Ahab. When Jezebel hunted the Lord's prophets, he sheltered and fed them. Later he became a follower of Elijah and received the gift of prophecy. His short book foretells the salvation of the Gentiles. He was buried in Samaria.

forefeast-entrance-theotokos.life: The Forefeast of the Entrance (Entry) of the Theotokos into the Temple prepares the faithful for the feast on 21 November. Tradition holds that Joachim and Anna, keeping a vow, brought the three-year-old Mary to the Jerusalem Temple, where the high priest Zachariah led her into the Holy of Holies. Hymns of the forefeast begin to announce this event.

afterfeast-entrance-theotokos.life: This is the afterfeast of the Entrance of the Theotokos into the Temple, celebrated on 21 November. According to tradition, Joachim and Anna fulfilled their vow by bringing the three-year-old Mary to the Temple. She climbed its steps unaided and was led by the high priest into the Holy of Holies. The Church sees in the event a sign of God's blessing and the coming of Christ.

alypius-stylite.life: Alypius was born at Adrianopolis in Paphlagonia and educated by Bishop Theodore. Guided by a vision of the martyr Euphemia, he built a church in her name and lived on a pillar beside it for fifty-three years, praying and teaching visitors. Two monasteries, for men and for women, arose around him under his direction. He died in 640 and was buried in that church.

stephen-younger.life: Stephen was born at Constantinople in 715 and, from age sixteen, lived as a monk on Mount Auxentius in Bithynia, where he later became abbot. He opposed the iconoclasm of Emperor Constantine V, was slandered, exiled, then imprisoned. There he led fellow confessors in prayer and was put to death by soldiers for his defense of icons.

martyr-paramon.life: Paramon was a local man of Bithynia who openly denounced the governor Aquianus for persecuting Christians. In 250, under Emperor Decius, the governor had imprisoned 370 Christians and urged them to sacrifice to idols. After tortures Paramon was beheaded together with all 370. The Church remembers them as martyrs of the Decian persecution.

prophet-nahum.life: Nahum, the seventh of the Twelve Minor Prophets, came from Elkosh in Galilee and lived in the seventh century B.C. His book foretells the fall of Nineveh, the Assyrian capital, which occurred in 612 B.C. OCA notes that few details of his life are known; he is said to have died at forty-five and been buried in his native region.

prophet-habakkuk.life: Habakkuk, the eighth of the Twelve Minor Prophets, was of the tribe of Simeon and prophesied around 650 B.C. He foresaw the destruction of the Temple and the Babylonian Captivity and return. According to the account in Daniel 14, an angel carried him to Babylon to bring food to Daniel. He died at great age; his relics were found under Theodosius the Younger.

prophet-zephaniah.life: Zephaniah, the ninth of the Twelve Minor Prophets, was of the tribe of Simeon and a contemporary of Jeremiah. He lived at the royal court and preached repentance, helping King Josiah remove idol worship. His prophecy warned of calamities coming upon Judea and neighboring peoples, among them Gaza, Ascalon, Moab, Ammon and Nineveh.

patapius-thebes.life: Patapios was born at Thebes in Egypt and withdrew to the desert, where visitors sought his counsel and found hospitality. He later settled in a cell by the city wall of Constantinople, near the Blachernae church, and became known for healing the sick. OCA records the healing of a woman with cancer. He was buried in the church of Saint John the Baptist.

menas-hermogenes-eugraphus.life: Menas, sent by Emperor Maximian from Athens to Alexandria to quell unrest, instead preached Christ and converted many. The envoy Hermogenes, sent to try him, was himself won to the faith. Eugraphus, Menas's secretary, declared himself a Christian and was stabbed by the emperor, while Menas and Hermogenes were beheaded. Their relics were later taken to Constantinople.

lucy-syracuse.life: Lucy was born at Syracuse in Sicily during the reign of Diocletian. She gave her wealth to the poor and vowed virginity. A rejected suitor denounced her to the prefect Paschasius. Sentenced to a brothel and then to burning, she was preserved, and was finally killed by a sword. Tradition holds that she was blinded, and she is invoked for eye ailments.

prophet-haggai.life: Haggai, the tenth of the Twelve Minor Prophets, was of the tribe of Levi and prophesied under the Persian king Darius. After the Jews returned from Babylonian captivity, he urged them to rebuild the Second Temple at Jerusalem and proclaimed that the Messiah would appear there. He is believed to have been buried with the priests at Jerusalem.

sebastian-rome.life: Sebastian, born in Gaul and educated at Milan, was a secret Christian who commanded the imperial guard under Diocletian and Maximian. He encouraged imprisoned Christians to stand firm and led many to baptism. Shot with arrows and left, he recovered, then publicly rebuked the emperors and was clubbed to death. His companions in the account, including Nicostratus, Zoe and Tiburtius, also died as martyrs.

boniface-tarsus.life: Boniface was a servant of the Roman noblewoman Aglaia, with whom he had lived in sin. Sent east to bring back martyrs' relics, he reached Tarsus in Cilicia, openly confessed Christ before the judge, endured tortures and was beheaded. His companions returned his body to Rome, where Aglaia built a church over it, gave away her wealth and later became a nun.

forefeast-nativity.life: The Forefeast of the Nativity begins on 20 December and runs through the 24th. From this day the hymns of the Church turn to the coming birth of Christ at Bethlehem, many being adapted from the hymns of Holy Week. It is a time of preparation for the feast of the Nativity of the Lord.

forefeast-nativity-2.life: This is the second day of the Forefeast of the Nativity, which prepares the faithful for the birth of Christ at Bethlehem. The services of these days increasingly speak of the approaching Nativity. The same date also commemorates the Virgin Martyr Juliana of Nicomedia, who died in 304 after steadfastly refusing marriage to a pagan official.

forefeast-nativity-3.life: This is the third day of the Forefeast of the Nativity of Christ. The Church's hymns on these days anticipate the Lord's birth at Bethlehem and call the faithful to prepare to meet Him. The same date also commemorates the Great Martyr Anastasia, who aided imprisoned Christians in Diocletian's persecution.

ten-martyrs-crete.life: Theodulus, Saturninus, Euporus, Gelasius, Eunician, Zoticus, Pompius, Agathopus, Basilides and Evaristus, ten Christians from various cities of Crete, were brought before the governor Decius. They confessed Christ steadfastly, endured thirty days of torture and were beheaded under Emperor Decius. About a century later Saint Paul of Constantinople took their relics to Constantinople.

forefeast-nativity-4.life: This is the fourth day of the Forefeast of the Nativity of Christ, close to the feast itself. The hymns of the day, such as those at Compline, call the faithful to draw near in soul and body to Bethlehem and to behold the birth of the Lord. The same date also commemorates the Ten Martyrs of Crete.

anysia-thessalonica.life: Anysia lived at Thessalonica under the co-emperor Maximian. After her parents died she sold her goods, gave to the poor and lived by fasting and prayer. On her way to church a soldier tried to force her to a pagan festival; when she resisted and spoke of Christ, he killed her with his sword. Christians buried her near the city gate and built a chapel there.

melania-roman.life: Melania the Younger was born in Rome to a wealthy family and, with her husband Apinianus (Pinian), renounced worldly life after the deaths of their children. They sold their estates, aided the needy and monasteries across the empire, and settled in Jerusalem. She founded a convent on the Mount of Olives and a men's monastery, and died in 439.
